"turn and twist about," Middle English writhen (transitive) "twist or bend in the shape of a wreathe or coil," from Old English wriðan (transitive) "to twist or bend," earlier "to bind or fetter," from Proto-Germanic *writhanan, reconstructed in Watkins to be from PIE *wreit-, from root *wer- (2) "to turn, bend."
The intransitive sense, in reference to the body or limbs, "move or stir in a twisting or tortuous manner," in agony, emotion, or grappling, is attested from c. 1300. Occasionally from Middle English, and especially 16c., "turn, change, tend (toward sin, etc.)." Related: Writhed; writhing.
Germanic cognates include North Frisian wrial, Old High German ridan, Old Norse riða, Middle Swedish vriþa, Middle Danish vride.

wrong.x:
late Old English, "twisted, crooked, wry" (senses now obsolete), from Old Norse rangr, earlier *vrangr "crooked, wry, wrong," from Proto-Germanic *wrang-, a nasalized variant of *wergh- "to turn," which according to Watkins is from PIE root *wer- (2) "to turn, bend."
Germanic cognates include Danish vrang "crooked, wrong," Middle Dutch wranc, Dutch wrang "sour, bitter," literally "that which distorts the mouth." Wrong thus would be etymologically a negative of right (adj.1), which is related to Latin rectus, literally "straight."*
The sense of "not right, bad, immoral, unjust, deviating from what is right or proper" developed by c. 1300. The meaning "not in accordance with reality" is by mid-14c.; of persons, "in a state of misconception or error," by early 15c. It is by mid-14c. as "less desirable or suitable" (of two).
As an adverb from c. 1200, "not rightly, incorrectly." To go wrong is in Shakespeare. Related: Wrongness; wrongish (1849).

late Old English, "that which is improper or wicked," from wrong (adj.). The meaning "an unjust action or anything contrary to right or justice" is recorded from c. 1200.
To be in the wrong "acting or being wrongly" is by c. 1400; phrase the wrong for "that which is wrong" is attested from c. 1300.
"do harm or injustice to," early 14c., wrongen, from wrong (adj.). Related: Wronged; wronging.

wroth.x:
Middle English, from Old English wrað "angry, irate" (literally "tormented, twisted"), from Proto-Germanic *wraith- (source also of Old Frisian wreth "evil," Old Saxon wred, Middle Dutch wret, Dutch wreed "cruel," Old High German reid, Old Norse reiðr "angry, offended"), whish is reconstructed in Watkins to be from *wreit-, from PIE root *wer- (2) "to turn, bend."
Related: Wrothly; wrothful; wrothy. It was apparently rare or obsolete from early 16c. to mid-19c. but has somewhat revived since, especially in dignified writing.
To wax wroth "grow irate" is by late 15c.

wrought.x: "worked" into shape or condition, early 12c., in fulwroht "fully done;" past-participle adjective from Middle English werken (see work (v.)). Especially "worked" as distinguished from rough in masonry, carpentry, etc. Wrought-iron (1703) is that which is malleable and has been brought into some form.

wry.x:
1520s, of the neck, face, features, "abnormally bent, distorted, somewhat twisted to one side," from obsolete verb wry "to contort, to twist or turn the neck, deviate from a straight course," Middle English wrien, from Old English wrigian "to turn, bend, move, go," from Proto-Germanic *wrig-.
This is reconstructed in Watkins to be from PIE *wreik- "to turn" (source also of Greek rhoikos "crooked," Lithuanian raišas "lame, limping"), from root *wer- (2) "to turn, bend."
Figuratively, of words, thoughts, etc., "devious in course or purpose, ill-natured," from 1590s. In reference to a smile by 1883. The original sense is preserved in awry.
Germanic cognates include Old Frisian wrigia "to bend," Middle Low German wrich "turned, twisted." Related: Wryness.

wunderkind.x: child prodigy (especially in music), 1883 in English (earlier as a German word in German contexts), from German Wunderkind, literally "wonder-child." For first element see wonder (n.). Second is German Kind "child" (see kind (n.)).

wurst.x: German-style sausage, by 1855, from German Wurst, from Old High German wurst "sausage," probably etymologically "mixture" (Watkins), from Proto-Germanic *wursti-, from PIE *wers- (1) "to confuse, mix up" (see war (n.)).

wynn.x: runic letter in Old English and early Middle English, representing "w;" Old English wyn, so called for being the first letter of that word, which means "delight, pleasure," from Proto-Germanic *wunjo-, from suffixed form of PIE root *wen- (1) "to desire, strive for."

wyvern.x: c. 1600, in heraldry, formed (with unetymological -n) from Middle English wiver, wyver (c. 1300), from Anglo-French wivre, from Old North French form of Old French guivre "poisonous snake," from Latin vipera "viper" (see viper). In heraldry, a winged dragon with eagle's feet and a serpent's barbed tail. For unetymological -n, compare bittern, slattern.

wife.x:
Middle English wif, wyf, from Old English wif (neuter) "woman, human female, lady," also in late Old English, "female partner in a sanctioned union" (wedded wife). This is from Proto-Germanic *wīfa- (source also of Old Saxon, Old Frisian wif, Old Norse vif, Danish and Swedish viv, Middle Dutch, Dutch wijf, Old High German wib, German Weib), a word of uncertain origin and disputed etymology, not found in Gothic.
The general sense of "woman" was long preserved in provincial English and is in midwife, old wives' tale (old wife "elderly woman," often a term of disparagement, is by c. 1200). The sense of "mistress of a household" (late 14c.) survives in housewife; and the later restricted sense of "tradeswoman of humble rank" in fishwife.
Apparently felt as inadequate in its basic sense, leading to the more distinctive formation wifman (source of woman).
The more usual Indo-European word is represented in English by queen/quean. Words for "woman" also double for "wife" in some languages. Some proposed PIE roots for wife include *weip- "to twist, turn, wrap," perhaps with sense of "veiled person" (see vibrate); and more recently *ghwibh-, a proposed root meaning "shame," also "pudenda," but the only examples of it would be the Germanic words and Tocharian (a lost IE language of central Asia) kwipe, kip "female pudenda."
Dutch wijf now means, in slang, "girl, babe," having softened somewhat from earlier sense of "bitch." The Modern German cognate (Weib) also tends to be slighting or derogatory; Middle High German wip in early medieval times was "woman, female person," vrouwe (Frau) being retained for "woman of gentle birth, lady;" but from c. 1200 wip "took on a common, almost vulgar tone that restricted its usage in certain circles" and largely has been displaced by Frau.
It is attested by 1883 as "passive partner in a homosexual couple." Wife-swapping "interchange of marital partners" is attested by 1954.
"take a wife, marry," late 14c., rare, from wife (n.).

Washington.x: U.S. capital, founded 1791, named for President George Washington (1732-1799); the family name is from a town in northeastern England, from Old English, literally "estate of a man named Wassa." The U.S. state was named when it was formed as a territory in 1853 (admitted to the union 1889). Related: Washingtonian.

wonder.x:
Middle English, from Old English wundor "strange or marvelous thing, unheard of or supernatural event; object of astonishment," from Proto-Germanic *wundran (source also of Old Saxon wundar, Middle Dutch, Dutch wonder, Old High German wuntar, German wunder, Old Norse undr), a word of unknown origin.
By late Old English as "cause of perplexity, a conundrum." In Middle English it also came to mean the emotion of amazement or reverential awe excited by novelty or something extraordinary and not well understood (late 13c.). By mid-14c. as "a spectacle."
To be no wonder "no surprise" was in late Old English (næs nan wunder, with emphatic negatives). A nine-days wonder (1590s) "subject of astonishment and gossip for a short time," was later "generally a petty scandal" (Century Dictionary); in Chaucer nine-nights wonder (compare nine). The original wonder drug (1939) might have been Sulfanilamide.

Middle English wondren, from Old English wundrian "be astonished, be struck with amazement," also "admire; make wonderful, magnify," from the source of wonder (n.) and like it of unknown origin. Germanic cognates include Dutch wonderen, Old High German wuntaron, German wundern.
The transitive sense of "be puzzled, be curious about, entertain some doubt, speculate expectantly," is attested by late Old English, hence I wonder for "I should like to know." Related: Wondered; wondering.
Reflexive dative use (I wonder me) was common in Middle English and as late as Tyndale (1533), and is said to survive in Yorkshire/Lincolnshire. It wonders me "it affects or strikes me with wonder" is attested by 1550s; its modern use in Pennsylvania German areas it is idiomatic, from German das wundert mich.

weapon.x:
Middle English wepen, from Old English wæpen (Anglian wæpen, Northumbrian woepn) "instrument of fighting and defense, sword," also figuratively, of spiritual combat, also "penis," from Proto-Germanic *wēipna- (source also of Old Saxon wapan, Old Norse vapn, Danish vaaben, Old Frisian wepin, Middle Dutch wapen, Old High German wafan, German Waffe "weapon"), a word of unknown origin with no cognates outside Germanic; possibly a substratum word. Related: Weaponed.
By c. 1300 of things not made as weapons but of service in a contest or struggle. Weapons-grade is by 1961 in reference to material for nuclear bombs.

worldwide.x: also world-wide, "as wide as the world, extending over the whole world," 1630s, from world (n.) + wide (adj.).

weekend.x:
also week-end, "holiday period at the end of a week," 1630s, from week + end (n.). Originally a northern word and referring to the period from Saturday noon to Monday morning; it became general after 1878 and by end of 19c. generally included all of Saturday.
As an adjective, "only on weekends," it is recorded from 1935. Long weekend is attested from 1900; in retrospective reference to Great Britain in the period between the world wars, 1944.
As a verb, "spend the weekend," by 1902; weekender for one who customarily spends the time away from home is by 1880. Related: Weekending.

whilst.x: by c. 1400, a variant (with unetymological -t, for which see amidst) of whiles (conj.) "during the time that" (mid-12c.), itself a variant of while (q.v.) in all its senses, with adverbial genitive -s-.

whereby.x: c. 1200, wher-bi, "along which, through which;" late 14c., "by what means, by which, how;" from where (in the sense of "in which position or circumstances") + by.

wireless.x:
by 1862 of unstrung pianos, 1886 of bustles; by 1876 in reference to telegraphy and attempts to send signals without the use of wires (water was tried as a medium; on railway systems the rails themselves); from wire (n.) + -less.
Marconi's system went into use in 1897 and was instantly celebrated, and the word came to be applied to it. By 1900 it was applied to the still newer technology of sending articulate sounds (wireless telephony) and thus to radio sound broadcasting. Hence, as a noun, "radio broadcasting" (by 1903) "radio set" (by 1921).
Both subsequently were superseded by classically derived (and thus international) radio. The international agreement and protocol on wireless (Berlin, 1906) uses radio-telegraphy and radio:
 "Wireless telegrams shall show in the preamble that the service is "wireless" ("radio")."
In early 1910s communications systems often are described as radio or wireless.

workforce.x: "workers or employees collectively," by 1947, from work (n.) + force (n.). Workfolk (late 15c.) was "farm laborers."

wherein.x: "in or within which or what," c. 1200, from where (in the sense of "in which position or circumstances") + in. By mid-14c. as "by which, through which." Similar formation in Dutch waarin, German worin, Swedish vari, Danish hvori. Related: Whereinsoever; whereinto.

weary.x:
Middle English weri, from Old English werig "tired, exhausted; dispirited by trouble, heartsick," related to worian "to wander, totter," from Proto-Germanic *worigaz (source also of Old Saxon worig "weary," Old High German wuorag "intoxicated"), a word of unknown origin.
The sense of "discontented with a continual recurrence" is by c. 1200. Related: Wearily.
Middle English werien, from Old English wergian "be or become tired" (intransitive), gewergian "to exhaust, to make tired" (transitive), from the source of weary (adj.). Related: Wearied; wearying.

wildlife.x: also wild life, "native fauna (and flora) of a region," 1879, from wild (adj.) + life. Earlier, wild life in book titles referred to accounts of living outdoors or among uncivilized peoples.

Welsh.x:
Middle English Welsh, from Old English Wielisc, Wylisc (West Saxon), Welisc, Wælisc (Anglian and Kentish) "foreign; British (not Anglo-Saxon), Welsh, native of Wales" (Celtic land which maintained its independence from England until 1282-3); also "not free, servile;" from Wealh, Walh "Celt, Briton, Welshman, non-Germanic foreigner."
In Tolkien's definition, "common Gmc. name for a man of what we should call Celtic speech," but also applied in continental Germanic languages to speakers of Latin, hence Old High German Walh, Walah "Celt, Roman, Gaulish," and Old Norse Val-land "France," Valir "Gauls, non-Germanic inhabitants of France" (Danish vælsk "Italian, French, southern"). It is from Proto-Germanic *Walkhiskaz, from a Celtic tribal name represented by Latin Volcæ (Caesar) "ancient Celtic tribe in southern Gaul."
As a noun, "the Britons," also "the Welsh language," both in Old English.
The Germanic adjective also survives in Wales, Cornwall, Walloon, walnut, and in surnames Walsh and Wallace. It was borrowed in Old Church Slavonic as vlachu, and applied to the Romanians, hence Wallachia.
Among the English, Welsh was used disparagingly of inferior or substitute things (such as Welsh cricket "louse" (1590s); Welsh comb "thumb and four fingers" (1796), and compare welch (v.)). Welsh mutton (1771), however, from sheep raised in Wales, was a choice delicacy.
Welshry "the Welsh collectively" is from mid-14c.

Wisconsin.x:
organized as a U.S. territory 1836; admitted as a state 1848. Originally applied to the Wisconsin River; a native name of unknown origin. Early spellings include Mescousing and Wishkonsing. "Of all the states of the American union, none has a name that has been spelled in more ways or interpreted more variously, than Wisconsin," according to Virgil J. Vogel, "Indian Names on Wisconsin's Map" (University of Wisconsin Press, 1991). He lists 15 spellings and says the word has been attributed to French, Menominee, Ojibwa, Potawatomi, Sauk-Fox, and Winnebago.
It was Wisconsan on an 1823 map of Michigan Territory; the modern spelling dates to 1829, but Wiskonsin remained a stubborn variant until the territorial legislature fixed the spelling in 1845.
Modern scholarship seems to look to the writings of Marquette (1670s) and his use of Mascouten, etc., for a river and people name. Vogel describes the theory:
 The Foxes' tribal name is Mesquackie, also spelled Meskwaki, Miscoquis, Miskwkeeyuk, Muskwaki, Musquakie, etc. The name means "red earth," deriving from the Fox tradition that they were created of red earth by the Great Spirit. The French called them Renards [Foxes] because they mistook a clan name for the tribal name. There is a remarkable resemblance between Marquette's 
 Mescousing and the name Mesquakie. The terminal 
 -akie in the tribal name means "earth," and the terminal 
 -ing in 
 Meskousing means "place." It is possible that the original term was 
 Meskwa ("red, inanimate") 
 aki ("earth") 
 ing ("place"). Marquette could have shortened it.

withdrawn.x: 1610s, "secluded," past-participle adjective from withdraw (v.). By 1713 in reference to a mental state of detachment.

Wayne.x: surname, by 1319, variant of Wain, representing wainwright, wainer (see wain) or perhaps "one who dwells by the tavern with the sign of the wain."

wanna.x: representing the casual pronunciation of want to, by 1896; wanta is by 1894.

wheelchair.x: also wheel-chair, "chair on wheels," used by invalids, etc., c. 1700, from wheel (n.) + chair (n.). Adjectival phrase wheelchair-bound, now discouraged, in reference to one who uses a wheelchair, is attested by 1981.

writ.x: Old English writ "that which is written, piece of writing," from the past participle stem of writan (see write). Used in reference to documents or instruments under seal of legal authority by early 12c.

woodland.x: Middle English wodeland, "woods, forest, wilderness," from Old English wudulond; see wood (n.) + land (n.). As an adjective, "of, peculiar to, or inhabiting the woods," from mid-14c. Related: Woodlander.

Wyoming.x:
region in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, from Munsee Delaware (Algonquian) chwewamink "at the big river flat," from /xw-/ "big" + /-e:wam-/ "river flat" + /-enk/ "place." Popularized by 1809 poem "Gertrude of Wyoming," set amid wars between Indians and American settlers, written by Scottish author Thomas Campbell (1777-1844), who seems to have accented it WY-o-MING and had a vague notion of Pennsylvania geography:
 On Susquehanna's side, fair Wyoming!
 Although the wild-flower on thy ruin'd wall,
 And roofless homes, a sad remembrance bring,
 Of what thy gentle people did befall;
 Yet thou wert once the loveliest land of all
 That see the Atlantic wave their morn restore.
 Sweet land! may I thy lost delights recall,
 And paint thy Gertrude in her bowers of yore,
 Whose beauty was the love of Pennsylvania's shore!
et cetera. Subsequently applied 19c. to other locations (in Kansas, Ohio, and Wisconsin), and to a western territory organized July 25, 1868, admitted as a state 1890.
 On the same day there was debate in the Senate over the name for the new Territory. Territories often keep their names when they become States, so we may be glad that "Cheyenne," to be pronounced "Shy-en," was not adopted. "Lincoln" was rejected for an obvious and, no doubt, sound reason. Apparently, nobody had a better name to offer, though there must be plenty of Indian words that could properly be used, and, for the present, the insignificant "Wyoming" is retained. [The Nation, June 11, 1868]

wow.x: 1510s, Scottish, a natural expression of amazement. "This old interjection had a new popularity in the early 1900s and again during the 1960s and later" [Dictionary of American Slang].
"overwhelm with delight or amazement," 1924, American English slang ("Variety"), from wow (interj.). Related: Wowed; wowing. As a noun meaning "unqualified success" by 1920.

whim.x: 1640s, "play on words, pun" (a sense now obsolete), shortened from whimwham "fanciful object" (q.v.). The meaning "caprice, fancy, sudden turn or inclination of the mind" is attested by 1690s, probably a shortened form of whimsy, which is of the same obscure family. Beaumont and Fletcher have dismissive whimling "person full of whims."

waterfront.x: also water-front, "land or buildings along a river, shore, etc.; the water-side of a city or town," 1834, American English, from water (n.1) + front (n.). To cover the waterfront "deal with thoroughly" is attested from 1913; I Cover the Waterfront was a 1932 best-seller by San Diego newspaperman Max Miller.

wallpaper.x: also wall-paper, "sturdy paper decorated in color or ornamental designs, for pasting on the walls of rooms," 1827, from wall (n.) + paper (n.).

whiff.x:
weffe, "foul scent or odor," 13c., of imitative origin.
The modern word is likely a fresh coinage based on the arrival of tobacco from the New World: "slight puff or gust of wind or air, also "an inhalation of tobacco smoke" (1590s). Probably influenced by whiffle "blow in gusts or puffs" (1560s).
The figurative sense of "a flavor, a hint or scent" is by 1872. The verb in the slang sense "swing at a ball and miss" is recorded by 1913 in baseball. Hence, generally, as a noun, "a failure." Related: Whiffed; whiffer; whiffing.

wistful.x:
1610s, perhaps but not certainly meaning "closely attentive" (in a verse line about songs that "should charm the sweet dale and wistfull hill."). The meaning "longingly pensive, musing" is attested by 1714.
It is perhaps from obsolete wistly "intently" (c. 1500), which is of uncertain origin. Perhaps it was formed on the model of wishful, but it is not considered to be a variant of it. It seems unrelated to wist (v.).
Middle English wistful meant "bountiful, well-supplied," from Old English wist "provisions." Related: Wistfully; wistfulness.

wad.x:
early 15c., wadde, "small bunch of fibrous, soft material for padding or stuffing," a word of uncertain origin, perhaps from Medieval Latin wadda (14c., source also of French ouate, Italian ovate), or Dutch watten (source of German Watte), or Middle English wadmal (c. 1300) "coarse woolen cloth," which perhaps is from Old Norse vaðmal "a woolen fabric of Scandinavia," probably from vað "cloth" + mal "measure."
The meaning "something bundled up tightly" (especially paper currency) is from 1778. To shoot (one's) wad "do all one can do" is recorded by 1860. The immediate source of the expression probably is wad in the sense of "disk of cloth used to hold powder and shot in place in a gun" (1660s). Wad in the slang sense of "a load of semen" is attested from 1920s, and the expression now sometimes is felt in this sense.
As a suffix, -wad in 1980s joined -bag, -ball, -head, -job as interchangeable second elements in combinations meaning "disgusting or unpleasant person."

1570s, "put a wad into," from wad (n.). From 1670s as "form into a wad;" 1759 as "pad or stuff with wadding," especially "line (a garment, etc.) with wadding to give roundness and fullness to the figure." Related: Wadded; wadding.

whirl.x:
c. 1300, whirlen, "move with a circular motion; go swiftly; move erratically;" probably from Old Norse hvirfla "to go round, spin," related to hvirfill "circle, ring, crown," and to Old English hweorfan "to turn" (see wharf). Related: Whirled; whirling.
Whirler (n.) is by mid-15c. as "person who whirls" (of dervishes, etc.); by 1860 in reference to revolving mechanisms. Colloquial whirlybird "helicopter" is attested from 1945 in U.S. military jargon.

early 15c., "flywheel of a spindle" (a sense now obsolete), from whirl (v.). The meaning "act of whirling, rapid circular motion or movement" is recorded from late 15c.; that of "something that moves with rapid, rotating motion" is by 1540s.
The figurative sense of "confused activity" is recorded from 1550s (whirling as a verbal noun is from late 14c.). The colloquial sense of "tentative attempt" (with give) is attested from 1884, American English.

wan.x:
Old English wann "dark, dusky, lacking luster," of weather, water, etc.; c. 1300, "leaden, pale, gray" through disease or distress; according to Boutkan related to Old English wanian "make or become smaller gradually, diminish, decline, fade" (see wane).
The connecting notion is want of vivid coloration, hence its use of anything indeterminately grayish or of a gloomy, unwholesome look. It also sometimes was used of bruises (compare livid). By mid-14c. of heavenly bodies. Related: Wanly; wanness.

waterproof.x: also water-proof, of material, etc., "repelling water," 1725, from water (n.1) + proof (n.). The noun meaning "garment of waterproof material" is attested by 1799. The verb, "render impervious to water," is recorded by 1843. Related: Waterproofed; waterproofing.

whimsical.x: "full of or characterized by odd fancies or peculiar notions," 1650s; see whimsy + -ical. Related: Whimsically; whimsicalness; whimsicality.

workstation.x: also work-station, 1950, "location at which one step of manufacturing is carried out," from work (n.) + station (n.). The sense of "desk with a computer terminal and keyboard" is by 1972, then transferred to the terminal itself.

wisp.x:
late 13c., "handful or bundle of hay, grass, etc.," used for burning or cleaning or as a cushion; a word of uncertain origin, perhaps from an unrecorded Old English word cognate with Norwegian and Swedish visp "wisp," all of unknown origin.
It is sometimes said to be connected with whisk (which also is sometimes strenuously denied) or with Middle Low German and Middle Dutch wispel "a measure of grain." The meaning "thin, filmy portion" is attested by 1836. As a verb by 1590s, "rub down with a wisp."

wily.x: "subtle, cunning, crafty, full of wiles," c. 1300, wili, of a person; late 14c. in reference to an act or trick; from wile (n.) + -ly (1). Related: Wilily; wiliness. In 16c. English had wily-pie "cunning fellow."

whirlpool.x:
"circular eddy or current in a river or sea, place where water is in constant circular motion," 1520s, from whirl (v.) + pool (n.1). Old English had hwyrfepol and wirfelmere; whirl-pit is from c. 1500.
In reference to a type of bath fitted with jets, for therapy, relaxation, etc., by 1975.

widget.x: "gadget, small manufactured item," c. 1920, American English, probably an alteration of gadget, perhaps based on which it.

wiki.x: web page that can be edited by browsers, by 2002, abstracted from names of such sites (such as Wikipedia, launched January 2001), the original being WikiWikiWeb, introduced and named by Ward Cunningham in 1995, from Hawaiian wikiwiki "fast, swift."

wispy.x: "like a wisp," 1717, from wisp + -y (2). Related: Wispiness. Earlier adjective was wispen (1580s).

watt.x: practical unit of electrical power, proposed and formally adopted 1882, in honor of James Watt (1736-1819), Scottish engineer and inventor. The surname is from an old pet form of Walter and also is in Watson.

winner.x: "one who or that which earns, keeps, or produces wealth," late 14c. (c. 1200 as a surname), agent noun from win (v.). Also "unscrupulous profiteer" (mid-15c.), and "one who triumphs in a contest or game" (mid-15c.). Adjectival winner-take-all is attested from 1901.

worker.x:
mid-14c., werker, "laborer, toiler, performer, doer," agent noun from work (v.). By late 14c. as "maker, crafter." As a type of bee that performs labor and services for the hive community, 1747 (worker-bee is by 1816).
As "one employed for a wage," 1848. Old English had wyrcend "worker, laborer."

writer.x:
Old English writere "one who can write; clerk, scribe, copyist;" also "one who produces philosophical books or literary compositions;" agent noun from writan (see write (v.)).
By c. 1200 in reference to a writer of a letter. Also in Middle English "reporter of events and deeds, chronicler, translator." As a surname by late 13c. (Adam le Wrytar). The meaning "sign-painter" is from 1837. Writer's cramp, occupation-neurosis in the hand of one who writes much, is attested by 1843 (also scrivener's palsy); writer's block, periodic disability among those who write creatively or constructively, is so called by 1950.

whorl.x:
mid-15c., "the small flywheel of a spindle," a variant or alteration of whirl (n.).
The meaning "circular arrangement of leaves or flowers round a stem of a plant" is recorded by 1550s. Of seashells or other spiral structures, from 1828. Related: Whorled.

wile.x: late Old English, wil "deceitful stratagem, crafty trick, sly artifice," a word of uncertain origin; perhaps from Old North French *wile (Old French guile), or directly from a Scandinavian source (compare Old Norse vel "trick, craft, fraud," vela "defraud"). Perhaps ultimately related to Old English wicca "wizard" (see Wicca). Middle English Compendium offers three guesses. Also compare guile. Specifically "deceitful charms," late 14c. (wiles of women). The lighter sense of "amorous or playful trick" is from c. 1600.

late 14c., wilen, "to deceive, make a dupe of," from wile (n.). Related: Wiled; wiling.
The verb in the sense of "cause (time, etc.) to pass pleasantly, divert attention pleasantly" is attested by 1796, from confusion with while (v.).

women.x: plural of woman (q.v.), retaining the original vowel sound. Semi-phonetic spelling wimmin is attested by 1910.

written.x: c. 1300, "composed or preserved in writing;" 1580s, "formed with the pen;" past-participle adjective from write (v.).

widely.x: "extensively, in or to a wide degree," 1660s, from wide (adj.) + -ly (2). Simple wide has been used as an adverb since late Old English; Middle English also had widen (Old English widan) "through or over a wide area."

worn.x:
"impaired or affected by wear or use," c. 1500, from adjectival use of past participle of wear (v.), which is from Old English geworen.
Worn-out "completely tired, exhausted by use, made ineffective by overuse" is attested from 1610s in reference to clothing, etc.; c. 1700 in reference to persons.

woke.x: past tense and past participle of wake (v.). Also a Middle English form of weak.

wellness.x: "state of being in good health," 1650s, from well (adv.) + -ness.

wraith.x: 1510s, "specter, ghost, apparition in the exact likeness of a person," Scottish, a word of uncertain origin. Weekley and Century Dictionary suggest Old Norse vorðr "guardian" in the sense of "guardian angel." Klein points to Gaelic and Irish arrach "specter, apparition."

welt.x:
early 15c., a shoemaker's term for a leather strip stitched between the sole and upper, a word of uncertain origin, perhaps related to Middle English welten "to overturn, roll over" (c. 1300), from Old Norse velta "to roll" (related to welter (v.)).
Extended generally to a hem, border, or trim, often forming a rounded ridge. Hence any low, superficial ridge or swelling; the meaning "ridge on the skin from a wound" is by 1800.
"fix a welt or welts in," late 15c., from welt (n.). Colloquial sense of "beast severely, with or as with a stick, etc., by which welts may be raised" is by 1823.

"to roll, revolve," obsolete, Middle English welten "topple, fall over," from Old English wiltan, wieltan "overthrow, throw down, turn, revolve" (see welter (v.)). By 1620s as "be sunk or deeply involved in." Related: Welted; welting.

whelp.x: Middle English whelp, from Old English hwelp "young dog," from a Germanic root related to Old Saxon hwelp, Old Norse hvelpr, Dutch welp, German hwelf; of unknown origin. Now largely displaced by puppy. Also applied to wild animals (lions, seals, etc.), but in literal use especially of the dog. The transferred sense of "scamp, saucy or impertinent youth" is by early 14c.; by late 15c. generally for "young child."
c. 1200, whelpen, of a female animal, "produce young, bring forth whelps," from whelp (n.). Related: Whelped; whelping.

wheedle.x: "to entice by soft words; get by flattery;" 1660s, a word of uncertain origin, perhaps connected with a survival of Old English wædlian "to beg," from wædl "poverty" [OED 1989], or borrowed by English soldiers in the Thirty Years' War from German wedeln "wag the tail," hence "fawn, flatter" (compare adulation). Related: Wheedled; wheedling. Louisa Mae Alcott has wheedlesome.

wangle.x: 1918, "obtain something by trickery;" earlier "accomplish in an indirect or insidious way," 1888, originally British printer's slang for "fake by manipulation," a word of uncertain origin. Compare wangle "move loosely on a base" (1820). Perhaps it is an alteration of waggle, or of wankle (now dialectal) "unsteady, fickle," from Old English wancol (see wench (n.)). Brought into wider use by soldiers in World War I.

whenas.x: "at the time at which; in a case in which," early 15c., from when + as.

widowhood.x: "condition of being a widow," c. 1200, widwehede, from widow (n.) + -hood. Modifying or replacing Old English wuduwanhad "state of a woman who is unremarried after the death of a spouse."

wheelbarrow.x: also wheel-barrow, "barrow on one or more wheels," early 14c., whele-barowe, from wheel (n.) + barrow (n.1).

wolfish.x: "like or befitting a wolf, having the qualities or traits of a wolf," 1560s, from wolf (n.) + -ish. Earlier form was wolvish (mid-15c.). Related: Wolfishly; wolfishness. Wolfy (adj.) is attested by 1848.

worrier.x: 1530s, "animal that bites and attacks others," agent noun from worry (v.). By 1891 as "one who worries himself."

wittol.x: "compliant or complaisant cuckold," late 15c., witewold, probably from witen "to know" (see wit (v.)) + ending from noun cuckold (Middle English cokewold).

Wolof.x: African people of Senegal and Gambia. Also the name of the Niger-Congo language they speak, by 1745 in English.

whomever.x: objective case of whoever, early 14c.; see whom + ever. Related: Whomsoever.

willfully.x: also wilfully, late Old English wilfullice "of one's own free will, voluntarily," and in part fresh coinage from willful + -ly (2). The bad sense of "in a stubborn manner" is by late 14c.; that of "on purpose, deliberately, knowingly" is attested by early 15c.

warbler.x: 1610s, "one who or that whcuh warbles," agent noun from warble (v.). Also applied to many sorts of Old World songbirds and by 1783 extended to North American birds that resemble them in appearance but sing little.

woody.x:
late 14c., wodi, of places, "abounding in wood, overgrown with trees and shrubs," from wood (n.) + -y (2). Of plants, "having a stem of wood," from 1570s. Related: Woodiness. Old English had wudulic.
As a name for a kind of station wagon with wood panels, by 1961, U.S. surfer slang (real wood exterior panels were rare after 1951 and the last use of real wood was in the 1953 Buick Roadmaster Estate Wagon). Earlier it was "a wood-pigeon" (by 1947).
The slang meaning "erection" is attested by 1990 (for hardness).

walkable.x: of a distance, "that may be (comfortably) covered on foot," by 1799, from walk (v.) + -able. Earlier as "fit for walking on, capable of being walked on" (1736). Related: Walkability.

wampum.x: string of seashell beads used ornamentally and as money by Native Americans, 1630s, shortened from New England Algonquian wampumpeag (by 1620s in English), "string of white (shell beads);" said to be compounded from wab "white" + ompe "string" + plural suffix -ag.

wagtail.x:
c. 1500, name for a small bird that has its tail in continuous motion (late 12c. as a surname), earlier wagstart (mid-15c.), from wag (v.) + tail (n.). From 18c. as "a harlot," but this sense seems to be implied plainly, if punningly, in the Elizabethans:
 If therefore thou make not thy mistress a goldfinch, thou mayst chance to find her a wagtaile. [Lyly, "Midas," 1592]

wildfire.x:
late Old English wilde fyr "destructive fire, raging conflagration" (perhaps originally one caused by lightning); also "erysipelas, spreading skin disease;" see wild (adj.) + fire (n.).
It is attested from c. 1300 as "Greek fire," an artificial composition of highly flammable material used in warfare; also fire rained down from the sky as divine retribution. The figurative sense, in reference to rapid spread and destructive fury, is by late 14c.

winder.x: 1550s, "person who winds;" 1580s, "machine or apparatus for winding," agent noun from wind (v.1).

woodsy.x: "belonging to, associated with, or characteristic of woods," 1848, American English, from woods (see wood (n.)) + -y (2).

wolfsbane.x: also wolf's-bane, "aconite" (especially Aconitum lycoctonum), a somewhat poisonous plant growing widely in Europe, 1540s, from wolf (n.) + bane; a translation of Latin lycoctonum, from Greek lykotonon (from lykos "wolf" + base of kteinein "to kill"). Also known dialectally in English as badger's bane, hare's bane, bear's bane.

watery.x: Middle English wateri, "consisting of water vapor;" of lands, "characterized by much rain;" from Old English wæterig; see water (n.1) + -y (2). Of the eyes, "moist, abounding in tears," mid-15c. Related: Wateriness.

wo.x: as a cry of grief, dismay, etc., see woe. As a call to a horse to stop, see whoa.

whitethorn.x: the common hawthorn, c. 1300, from white (adj.) + thorn (n.).

walkabout.x: "periodic migration by a westernized Aboriginal into the bush," 1828, Australian English, from the verbal phrase (attested by c. 1300); see walk (v.) + about. By 1946 in reference to any protracted stroll or wandering visit.

Walloon.x:
1520s, in reference to a people of what is now southern and southeastern Belgium, also of their language, from French Wallon, literally "foreigner," a word of Germanic origin (compare Old High German walh "foreigner"), perhaps via Frankish.
The people are of Gaulish origin, descendants of the ancient Belgae, and speak a French dialect. The name is a form of the common appellation of Germanic peoples to Romanic-speaking neighbors. Compare Vlach, Wallach, also walnut and Welsh. As a noun from 1560s; as a language name from 1640s. In colonial New York, one of the Huguenot settlers from Artois in northeastern France.

Waterloo.x: village near Brussels; the great battle there took place June 18, 1815; extended sense of "a final, crushing defeat" is attested by Dec. 5, 1816 in letter of Lord Byron. The name is roughly "watery clearing;" the second element is from Flemish loo "forest clearing, sacred wood" (see lea (n.)).

wheeler.x: late 14c, "wheelwright, maker of wheels" (mid-13c. as a surname), from wheel (n.) + -er (1). Wheeler-dealer is from 1954, apparently a rhyming elaboration of dealer. To wheel and deal "engage in shrewd bargaining" is by 1961.

workbook.x: also work-book, "book of daily duties in a business," 1910, from work (n.) + book (n.). By 1932 in U.S. education as "book of problems to be worked out."

wheelie.x: 1966 as a bicycling stunt of riding on the rear wheel only with the front wheel elevated; from wheel (n.) + -ie.

wildcat.x:
also wild-cat, undomesticated European wild cat, one of the stock from which some domestic cats descended, early 14c., wilde cat (late 12c. as a surname), from wild (adj.) + cat (n.). In U.S. of a species of lynx. The meaning "savage woman" is recorded from 1570s.
The sense of "one who forms rash projects" is attested by 1812; the adjective in the financial speculative sense of "wild, reckless" is by 1838, American English, hence in a general sense of "sudden and unofficial" by 1880s. Related: Wildcatter; wildcatting.

woozy.x: "muddled or dazed, as with drink," 1897, American English colloquial, variant of oozy "muddy," or an alteration of boozy. It is recorded in 1896 as student slang, but with a sense "foolish, behind the times," also "pleasant, delightful."

wipeout.x:
also wipe-out, by 1921 as a condition in radio where one signal overrides a weaker, from the verbal phrase (see wipe (v.) + out (adv.)). Later as a separate formation "an act of being knocked off one's surfboard" by 1962, American English slang; also as a verb in this sense.
The verbal phrase wipe out is attested by mid-15c. as "erase;" earlier in this sense wipe typically was paired with away or off. As "destroy, obliterate," it is attested from c. 1600; of groups of persons, "put to death entirely" by 1861.

whereupon.x:
c. 1300, wher-upon, "upon which or whom, on which, whereon," from where (partly in the sense of "in which position or circumstances") + upon. By early 15c. as "following on which."
Perhaps felt as a fuller form of whereon, but where-up is attested in Middle English from late 13c., "anywhere," also "that said, on the basis of the foregoing."

woodlouse.x: also wood-louse, "sow-bug," 1610s, from wood (n.) + louse (n.). So called from being found in old wood. The name also is used of termites and death-watch beetles.

wainwright.x: "wagon-builder," Old English wægn-wyrhta; see wain + wright. Not in Middle English but surviving as a surname.

wooly.x:
also woolly, 1570s, "consisting of, resembling, or made of wool," from wool (n.) + -y (2).
The meaning "barbarous, rude" is by 1891, from American English wild and wooly, a phrase from the frontier, by 1878 a regular feature in journalistic accounts of the big talk of the Old West, probably suggestive of animal savagery:
 "I am a wolf from Bitter Creek, the further up you go, the worse they get, and I'm from the headwaters! Whoppee! Wild and wooly and full of fleas, and never was curried above my knees! Wake, snakes, and come at me! I'm a tarantula from Del Norte, a snapping turtle of the valley, and I eat men and animals!" ["Gold Hill Daily News," Nevada, Dec. 12, 1879]
quoted from St. Louis, shows the usual full form of it. Related: Wooliness. Wooly-haired is by 1791. The woolly bear caterpillar is so called by 1845, American English.

whyever.x: "for whatever reason," by 1856, from why + ever.

Whiggery.x: "principles or practices of the Whigs," 1680s, from Whig + -ery.

watercourse.x: also water-course, mid-15c., "channel for water, stream-bed;" from water (n.1) + course (n.). Earlier was water-gang (mid-13c.).

whopper.x:
"uncommonly large thing," 1767, colloquial, originally and especially "an audacious lie;" formed as if from whop (v.) "to beat, overcome." Whopping "large, big, impressive" is attested by 1620s.
For similar evolution, compare colloquial or slang smasher, slapper, buster, bumper; swapper "something very big" (1700), thumper "thing large and impressive of its sort" (1650s), thwacker "something big" (1670s), spanker (1751), whacker (1825), whaler "anything big" (by 1860, from whale (v.2) "beat severely"), yanker "a great lie" (1822); etc.
 The girl was not long in finding the melon, and in the eagerness of her joy she exclaimed, before she was near the house, "Oh law, daddy, its a roarer." [Anne Royall, "Sketches," 1826, anecdote from Knoxville, Tenn.]
For the present-participle adjectives, see strapping.

Westphalia.x:
German region, formerly a duchy (and from 1807-13 a Napoleonic kingdom), Middle English West-vale, Westevale, Westfalia, Westphale, Westfall; in 17c. Westphally; it is attested by late-14c., in reference to fabrics and cloths from there.
The second element is probably Germanic falah "field" (from PIE root *pele-  (2) "flat; to spread," thus related to Pole). There formerly also was an Ostphalia. The unetymological spelling with -ph- is by mid-15c.
The treaties ending the Thirty Years' War were signed in Westphalia on Oct. 24, 1648 (in Osnabrück and Münster). They ended the Catholic-Protestant military struggle in Europe, established diplomatic protocol and overall begat the modern international order based on nation-states. Hence Westphalian for the political ideology.
The region also was noted in 17c. England for the its bacon. hence Malevole's "sallow Westphalian gammon-faced zaza" (in Marston's "The Malcontent").

wrinkly.x: early 15c., wrinkli, in anatomy, "having a tendency to be wrinkled," from wrinkle (n.) + -y (2). As teen slang noun for "old person," by 1972 ("old" being relative; a British reference from 1982 applies it to people in their 40s).

worksheet.x: "paper with notes, etc., relating to a work in progress," 1909, from work (n.) + sheet (n.1). By 1966 as "list of exercises or problems to be worked out by students."

whitefish.x: collective name for cod, haddock, hake, sole, and other food fish of a white color, mid-15c., from white (adj.) + fish (n.).

wifehood.x: "married state, wedlock, wifely conduct," late 14c., wifhod; see wife (n.) + -hood. Old English wifhad meant "womanhood."

wordy.x: "prolix, garrulous, verbose," Middle English wordi, from Old English wordig; see word (n.) + -y (2). Related: Wordily; wordiness.

wormy.x: mid-15c., wormi, "infested with or full of worms," from worm (n.) + -y (2). Related: Worminess. Worm-like is from 1540s; worm-eaten from late 14c.

wastage.x:
"loss or diminution by use, wear, decay, etc.," 1670s, a hybrid from waste (v.) + -age.
wastage. It is possible that sentences may be constructed in which this word is for some reason better than waste ; what is certain is that in nearly all the places in which it nowadays appears it is not better. [Fowler, "Modern English Usage," 1926]

wanderer.x: mid-15c., wandrere, "one who travels about," agent noun from wander (v.).

whiplash.x:
also whip-lash, late 14c., whippes lash, "flexible strip used as a lash, the pliant part of a whip," from whip (n.) + lash (n.).
The injury caused by sudden head motion was so called colloquially by 1955, in reference to the notion of moving to and fro like a cracking whip. The verb in this sense is recorded by 1971.

witchcraft.x:
Middle English wicchecraft "sorcery, magic; occult arts as a subject of study," from Old English wiccecræft "witchcraft, magic," from wicce (see witch (n.)) + cræft "power, skill" (see craft (n.)). Also in Old English wiccedom.
Witchcraft was declared a crime in English law in 1542, at the beginning of the Protestant era; trials there peaked in the 1580s and 1640s but fell sharply after 1660. The last, in 1717, ended in acquittal. The Witchcraft Act was repealed 1736. Lecky ("Rationalism in Europe," 1866) examines Hutchinson and Buckle and concludes that belief in witchcraft and sorcery had been common in England even among the most educated at the time of the Restoration in 1660. By 1688, the majority disbelieved it; by 1718 the minority was reduced to the ignorant and an insignificant section of the clergy.

wigwam.x: tent or lodge (formed of bark or skins laid over poles) of some North American native peoples, 1620s, from Algonquian (probably Eastern Abenaki) wikewam "a dwelling," said to mean literally "their house;" also said to be found in such formations as wikiwam and Ojibwa wiigiwaam and Delaware wiquoam.

wildly.x: early 15c., wildeli, "in an unrestrained or furious way, extravagantly," from wild (adj.) + -ly (2).

waitress.x: "female waiter, woman who waits tables at a restaurant," 1834, also sometimes "waiting-maid" as a private servant; see waiter + -ess. Related: Waitressing, by 1936.

winkle.x: edible mollusk, 1580s, shortening of periwinkle (n.2). Winkler "one who gathers winkles for sale" is by 1889; as "one who assists in the eviction of tenants," by 1970.

weekday.x:
Middle English weke-dai, "one of the seven days of the week," but especially any day other than Sunday; from Old English wicudæge, wucudæge "day of the week" (similar formation in Old High German wehhatag, Old Norse vikudagr); see week + day.
Week-night, weeknight is attested by 1859. Also compare weekend. Archaic week's day was "day of last or next week corresponding to the present day."

waistband.x: "band meant to encircle the waist," especially as part of a garment to maintain or enhance firmness there, 1580s, from waist + band (n.1).

Whiggish.x: "of or pertaining to the Whigs or partaking of their principles," 1670s, from Whig + -ish. Whiggism is attested by 1680s.

whaler.x: 1680s, "person engaged in whale-hunting;" 1806 in reference to a vessel; agent noun from whale (v.1). Old English had hwælhunta.

waxwork.x:
"work in wax," especially artistic modeling of objects, 1690s, from wax (n.) + work (n.). Waxworks "exhibition of life-size wax figures representing famous or notorious persons" is recorded by 1796. Wax museum in the same sense is by 1817 (wax-work museum is from 1815).
 It is to be regretted that the growing interest in anatomical and physical studies has been perverted to vulgar ends by the unprincipled exhibitors of catch-penny wax museums, whose coarse transparencies and blatting horns offend the eyes and ears of decent people. [New York Independent, Feb. 7, 1850]

watermelon.x: vine-plant highly cultivated as a foodstuff, also its fruit, 1610s, from water (n.1) + melon. So called for being full of thin juice. Compare French melon d'eau. The modern sweet variety dates from Roman times. It was a garden-plant in Europe by 17c. and was introduced in the New World by 1570s by Spanish colonists.

whoremaster.x: also whore-master, mid-14c., "pimp, one who keeps or procures whores for others," from whore (n.) + master (n.).

wilful.x: British English spelling of willful. Related: Wilfully; wilfulness.

wrestler.x: "one who engages in formal grappling combat, competitive professional grappler," late Old English, agent noun from wrestle (v.).

woolen.x:
also woollen (chiefly British English), "made of or consisting of wool," Old English wullen, wyllen; see wool + -en (2).
As a noun, "cloth made or chiefly made of wool," c. 1300; woolens (woollens) "woolen manufactures" is by 1800.

wedgie.x: 1940, "wedge-heeled shoe," from wedge (n.) + -ie. The underwear prank so called by 1970s, from the effect it gives the victim.

waggle.x: late 15c. (implied in waggling), "cause to wag often," frequentative of wag (v.) with -el (3). Compare Dutch waggelen "to waggle," Old High German wagon "to move, shake," German wackeln "to totter." The transitive sense of "move with a wagging motion" is attested from 1590s. Related: Waggled. As a noun, "a sudden, short, side-to-side movement," by 1885.

windhover.x: "kestrel," 1670s, from wind (n.1) + hover; so called from the bird's habit of hovering in the wind. Among the many early names for it was windfucker (1590s).

widen.x: c. 1600 (transitive), "make (something) wide or wider," from wide (adj.) + -en (1). Intransitive sense of "grow wider" is by 1709. Simple wide was used as a verb from c. 1300. Related: Widened; widening.

windmill.x:
"mill powered by the wind," c. 1300 (mid-13c. in place names), wind-milne, from wind (n.1) + mill (n.). Similar formation in German Windmühle, Dutch windmolen, French moulin à vent. Figurative expressions of tilting at (or fighting with) windmills (1640s) are from "Don Quixote."
The verb meaning "swing the arms wildly" is recorded from 1888. Related: Windmilled; windmilling.

waterboy.x: also water-boy, "boy who brings round drinking water," by 1859, from water (n.1) + boy (n.).

whammo.x: exclamation signifying violence or surprise at a heavy blow, 1932, from wham (q.v.) + -o.

whammy.x: often double whammy, "hex, evil eye," 1932, of unknown origin, popularized 1941 in Al Capp's comic strip "Li'l Abner," where it was the specialty of Evil-Eye Fleegle.

wester.x:
"tend or go west, travel westward," late 14c., westren, of the sun, moon, and stars in the sky, from west (adv.), and compare westerly. Related: Westered; westering.
Verbal noun westering "setting of the sun, westward declination of a star" was in Middle English (early 15c.).

welterweight.x:
by 1831 in reference to unusually heavy weight carried by certain horses in a steeplechase or hurdle races," from earlier sense of "heavyweight horseman;" from weight (n.) + welter "heavyweight horseman" (1804). This is of uncertain origin, possibly from an early use of colloquial welt (v.1) "beat severely." Later "boxer or wrestler of a certain weight" (1896).
 ... but at the end of the first German mile, Nature gave way, and this excellent mare was obliged to "knock under" to the extraordinary exertions she had made, and to the welter weight she carried, upwards of 13 stone. [The Sporting Magazine, September 1831]
Compare welter-stakes, "race for heavyweight riders" (1820). By 1865 in colloquial use for anything big or heavy of its kind.

wrasse.x: type of salt-water fish, 1670s, from Cornish wrach, related to Welsh gurach.

wieldy.x: late 14c., weldi, "capable of wielding," from wield (v.) + -y (2). The meaning "capable of being wielded" is attested by mid-15c., now perhaps archaic. Old English had wielde "powerful, victorious." Related: Wieldiness. Wieldless "unmanageable" is from 1550s but rare.

watchtower.x: also watch-tower, "tower from which a sentinel watches for enemies or danger, look-out tower," 1540s, from watch (n.) + tower (n.).

winery.x: "establishment for making wine," 1867, American English, from wine (n.) + -ery. Middle English had vintrie "place where wine is sold" (c. 1300).

wickedness.x: c. 1300, wikkedness, "moral evil, state or condition of being addicted to vice," from wicked + -ness. Middle English also had wikkedhede.

wherewithal.x: "with which," 1530s; see where + withal ("with all"). Or perhaps in part wherewith (q.v.) + -al (2). Used colloquially as a noun, "the means (to do something), what is necessary or required" by 1809. Middle English had therewithal (adv.) "using that, with that; in addition to that, besides," and other similar formation.

wherry.x: "light, shallow rowboat," used chiefly in rivers and harbors, mid-15c., wheri, a word of unknown origin. Related: Wherryman.

woofer.x: "loudspeaker for bass notes," 1935, imitative agent-noun (compare woof (n.2)).

whistler.x: Middle English whistlere, "one who plays in a pipe," from Old English hwistlere "piper," literally "whistler," agent noun from hwistlian (see whistle (v.)). Of birds with a whistling note, by 1580s.

waveless.x: "free from waves, undisturbed," 1590s, from wave (n.) + -less. Related: Wavelessly; wavelessness.

warcraft.x: "military science, cunning in warfare, the art of war," c. 1400, from war (n.) + craft (n.).

wegotism.x:
"an obtrusive and too frequent use of the first person plural by a speaker or writer" [OED, 1989], from we + egotism. Coined in 1797:
 ... which, if we did not too much respect etymology, we might jocularly style Wegotism. [review of John Ireland, "Five Discourses," in British Critic, April, 1797]
Mock his we-ship is attested from 1670s.

watercress.x: perennial creeping herb of springs and streams, from antiquity used as a spring salad and in medicinal remedies, also water-cress, c. 1300, water-cresse, from water (n.1) + cress. Compare Middle Low German, Middle Dutch waterkerse, German wasserkresse.

westward.x: "to or toward the west, in a westerly direction," Old English westweard; see west + -ward. Also westwards, with adverbial genitive. As an adjective, "western, westerly, being toward the west," by c. 1200. Westward, ho! meaning "to the west" was the old cry of Thames boatmen hailing passengers going west from the city.

westernization.x:
also westernisation, 1873, noun of action from westernize (v.). Earliest reference is to Japan.
 [The mikado's] late rapid and radical progress in westernization (to evolve a word that the Japanese will need) justifies great expectations of him. [Coates Kinney, "Japanning the English Language," The Galaxy, July-Dec. 1873]

wherefore.x: "for that cause or reason, on account of which," c. 1200, wher-fore, hwarfore, from where (in the sense of "in which position or circumstances") + for (prep.). Similar formation in Dutch waarvoor, Old Norse hvar fyrir, Swedish varfor.

wiener.x: 1900, shortening of wienerwurst (1874, American English), from German Wiener "of Vienna" (from Wien; see Vienna) + Wurst "sausage" (see wurst). Colloquial wienie is attested by 1911 (see weenie). The extensive pejorative senses seem to have developed from its penis-like shape. Also compare weeny. Wiener roast is attested by 1910.

wireman.x: worker on electrical lines, 1881, from wire (n.) + man (n.). Earlier "one who makes wires, a wire-drawer" (1540s).

wombat.x: marsupial mammal of Australia, 1798, from Aboriginal womback, wombar.

wattage.x: electrical power expressed in watts, 1897, from watt + -age.

wideness.x: "lineal extent from side to side; state of being wide," Old English widness; see wide (adj.) + -ness, and compare width.

wildwood.x: also wild-wood, late Old English wilde wode "natural forest, unfrequented and trackless woods;" see wild (adj.) + wood (n.).

windage.x: 1710, "allowance of space between the projectile and the diameter of the tube of a firearm," from wind (n.1) + -age. Meaning "allowance for wind deflection" is from 1867.

westbound.x: also west-bound, "travelling west," by 1866, American English, originally in railroading, from west + bound (adj.2).

waywiser.x: "instrument for measuring distances of a rolling wheel on a road," 1650s; see way (n.) + wise (n.). The compound in continental Germanic languages tends to mean "guide, directory" (Dutch wegwijzer, German Wegweiser, Danish vejviser, etc.).

whereabouts.x:
late 14c., wher-aboutes, "at what business," early 15c., from where (in the extended sense of "concerning which") + about, with adverbial genitive -s.
The noun meaning "place where someone or something is," is recorded from 1795, probably from whereabout (adv.). Whereabout in the sense of "one's present place" is from c. 1600.

Wobbly.x: 1914, member of Industrial Workers of the World (I.W.W.). Probably an elaboration of the W aspect of the acronym.

Wellington.x: type of riding boot with the leg extended upward, by 1817, in reference to or honor of Arthur, 1st Duke of Wellington (1769-1852), the English hero of Waterloo, later a conservative political leader, who in life also had a style of coat, hat, and trousers named for him, as well as a chest of drawers, variety of apple, a baked steak dish, and giant evergreen tree (the last did not take in America; see sequoia). Related: Wellingtonian.

windbag.x: late 15c., wyndbagge, "bag filled with air; bellows for an organ," from wind (n.1) + bag (n.). The figurative sense of "person who talks too much" is attested from 1827.

wrongful.x: c. 1300, "full of or characterized by wrong; contrary to moral or religious teachings; unfair, unlawful, unjust;" from wrong (n.) + -ful. Related: Wrongfully; wrongfulness. Middle English had also the adjective wrongous, sometimes wrongeous, also wrong-wise.

whatness.x: 1610s, translating the Latin source of quiddity, from what + -ness.

witchy.x: "of the nature of or resembling a witch," 1660s, from witch (n.) + -y (2). Related: Witchiness.

wingtip.x: also wing-tip, "tip of a wing," by 1828 in reference to a bird (from 1825 in reference to a fairy); from wing (n.) + tip (n.1). Of airplane wings from 1909. As a type of shoe with a back-curving toe cap suggestive of a bird's wingtip, from 1928. Related: Wing-tipped.

weightless.x: "having no weight," 1540s, from weight (n.) + -less. Related: Weightlessly; weightlessness (1867).

westabout.x: "around toward the west," 1570s, from west + about.

watchful.x: "alert, vigilant," c. 1500, waccheful, from watch (n.) + -ful. Related: Watchfulness.

weeper.x: "one who weeps," especially "hired mourner," late 14c., agent noun from weep (v.). Also in 18c.-19c. something worn as a badge of mourning. The sense of "sentimental novel, story, etc." is from 1934.

windward.x: "on the side toward the point from which the wind blows," 1680s, from wind (n.1) + -ward. Related: Windwards. As a noun, point from which the wind blows," by 1510s.

welder.x: 1828, "one who welds;" 1896, "instrument or appliance for welding;" agent noun from weld (v.).

waddle.x: "to walk with short, ungainly steps, swaying from side to side; to walk as a duck does," 1590s, diminutive or frequentative of wade. (v.), with -el (3). Related: Waddled; waddler; waddling. The noun is recorded from 1690s, "act of waddling; a clumsy gait with short, toddling steps."

wavelet.x: "small wave, ripple," 1808, mainly in poetry, from wave (n.) + diminutive suffix -let.

wordcraft.x: Old English wordcræft "poetic art, eloquence;" see word (n.) + craft (n.). The modern word in the sense of "literary skill, art of using words well" might be a new formation.

wah-wah.x:
1926, in jazz slang, in reference to the effect on brass instruments made by manipulating the mute; of imitative origin. Later also in reference to an electric guitar effect. As an imitation of the sound of a baby crying, it is recorded from 1938. Wah-wah pedal is recorded from 1969.
Compare Chinook jargon wawa "talk, speak, call, ask, sermon, language;" Cree (Algonquian) wehwew "goose," Lenape (Algonquian) wava "snow goose," all probably of imitative origin, which yielded American English wavey, wavy "snow goose" (1795).

wall-to-wall.x: "extending from one wall of a room to the opposite," by 1939, of shelving, etc.; see wall (n.). The metaphoric sense (usually disparaging) is by 1967.

war-monger.x: also warmonger, "one who seeks to bring about war," 1580s, from war (n.) + monger (n.). First attested in Spenser's "Faerie Queene," and perhaps coined by him.

war-paint.x: "traditional markings painted on the face and body as a sign of going to war," 1826 (Fennimore Cooper), in reference to Native North Americans; see war (n.) + paint (n.). In 19c. colloquial use, "cosmetics; one's best clothes."

war-time.x: also war time, "time when war is being waged," late 14c., from war (n.) + time (n.).

warm-up.x:
"act or practice of lightly exercising or practicing before an activity," 1915; earlier in literal sense, "a heating" (of something), 1878, from verbal phrase warm up, which is attested by 1868 in the sense of "exercise before an activity."
The verbal phrase is attested from 1848 in reference to heating food; earliest use (c. 1400) is figurative, of persons, "become eager or animated." In reference to appliances, motors, etc., attested from 1947.

weather-vane.x: also weathervane, device to show the direction of the wind, mid-15c., wederfane; see weather (n.) + vane.

well-adjusted.x: 1735, in reference to mechanisms, etc., from well (adv.) + past participle of adjust (v.). In reference to emotional balance, by 1939.

well-balanced.x: "properly adjusted or regulated," 1620s, from well (adv.) + balanced.

well-behaved.x: "of good conduct, courteous, civil," 1590s, from well (adv.) + past participle of behave (v.).

well-beloved.x: "very dear, cherished; popular, respected," late 14c., wel-biloved, from well (adv.) + beloved. From early 15c. as a noun and in salutations.

well-done.x:
c. 1200, "rightly or appropriately done, wise, prudent," from well (adv.) + done. In reference to meat, "thoroughly cooked," by 1747.
Well done! as an exclamation of approval is recorded from mid-15c. Middle English also formed well-doer "one who behaves properly; well-doing "good, proper, or virtuous behavior."

well-dressed.x: "in becoming attire," 1570s, from well (adv.) + past participle of dress (v.).

well-earned.x: "thoroughly deserved," 1730, from well (adv.) + past participle of earn (v.).

well-hung.x: 1610s, in reference to male genitalia, from well (adv.) + hung (adj.). By 1762 as "suspended or attached so as to hang properly."

well-kept.x: "carefully preserved or stored," c. 1400, from well (adv.) + past participle of keep (v.).

well-meant.x: "rightly intended, friendly, sincere," late 15c., from well (adv.) + past participle of mean (v.).

well-ordered.x: "rightly regulated or governed," c. 1600, from well (adv.) + past participle of order (v.).

well-regulated.x: "in good order as to arrangement or control," 1709 (Shaftsbury), from well (adv.) + past participle of regulate (v.).

well-respected.x: "highly esteemed," 1590s, from well (adv.) + past participle of respect (v.).

well-wisher.x: "one favorably inclined" (to a person, cause, etc.), 1580s, from well (adv.) + agent noun from wish (v.). Well-wishing (n.) is recorded from 1560s; well-wish (n.) "favorable or benevolent desire" is from 1620s.

white-hot.x: "heated to full incandescence," 1820, from white (adj.) + hot (adj.). White heat is attested by 1710 as "degree at which bodies radiate white;" the figurative sense of "state of intense or extreme emotion" is attested by 1839.

white-out.x: 1946 as an extreme snow condition on the U.S. prairie, from white as a verb + out (adv.). From 1977 as a liquid correction for paper.

whoop-de-doo.x:
expression of excitement or enthusiasm, earliest as whoop-de-doodle-do (1854, as a song title), perhaps suggestive of a cock-crow (compare cock-a-doodle-doo). By 1879 as a noun, "noisy, enthusiastic nonsense" in politics, etc.
With variants including whoop-de-oodum-do (1857), whoop-de-dooden-do (1867); whoop-de-damn-do (by 1996, Derrick Coleman). Whoop-de-doo was the title of a 1903 Weber-and-Fields burlesque show.
The 1854 citation is in an account of boys hawking sheet music to popular songs on streets of New York, which mentions "Whoop-de-doodle-do" among the titles for sale. [Raleigh (N.C.) Register, Aug. 30, 1854].

wire-tapping.x: also wiretapping, "surreptitiously obtaining information by connecting wires to telegraph (later telephone) lines and establishing an intermediate station between two legitimate ones," 1878, from wire (n.) + agent noun from tap (v.2). Earliest references often are to activity during the American Civil War, but the phrase does not seem to have been used at that time. Related: Wire-tap; wire-tapper.

won't.x: contraction of will not, woll not, 1610s in verse plays. See will. Earlier as wynnot (mid-15c.), later wonnot (1580s). Compare shan't, don't.

work-up.x:
"diagnostic examination of a patient," 1961, from the verbal phrase; see work (v.) + up (adv.). To work up (transitive) "bring into some state or condition" is by 1590s of material things, 1690s of immaterial things; hence "bring by labor or special effort to a higher state or condition" (1660s).
From work (v.) in a sense of "excite by degrees" comes work up (v.) "excite, stir up, raise, rouse," c. 1600, and worked-up "mentally or emotionally agitated" (1903); wrought-up "stimulated" is from 1810.

Wisteria.x: also Wistaria, genus of woody vines, 1819, formed by Thomas Nuttall, English botanist, and named in recognition of American anatomist Caspar Wistar (1761-1818) of Philadelphia + abstract noun ending -ia. The form in -e- apparently is a misprint. The Wistar Institute was founded in 1892 by his great-nephew and named for him.

wingding.x: 1927, originally hobo slang, "counterfeit seizures induced to attract sympathy;" the meaning "energetic celebration" is by 1949. As a type of dingbat fonts made by Microsoft, from 1990.

witted.x: "possessed of intelligence or understanding;" late 14c. in compounds, "having wits" (of a certain kind), from wit (n.).

waisted.x: "fitted with a (specified type of) waist," c. 1400, from waist.

watering.x: Old English wæterunge "a carrying water; a sprinkling water" (on plants), verbal noun from water (v.). From late 14c. as "a soaking with water;" mid-15c. as "a giving water to (an animal);" c. 1600 as "salivation." In reference to running of the eyes by c. 1400. Watering-can is from 1690s (earlier water-can, late 14c.). Also see watering-hole.

weakling.x: "feeble creature," 1520s, coined by Tyndale from weak (adj.) + -ling as a loan-translation of Luther's Weichling "effeminate man" (from German weich "soft") in I Corinthians vi.9, where the Greek is malakoi, from malakos "soft, soft to the touch," "Like the Lat. mollis, metaph[oric] and in a bad sense: effeminate, of a catamite, a male who submits his body to unnatural lewdness" ["Thayer's Greek-English Lexicon of the New Testament," 1889].

wooded.x: "covered with growing trees," c. 1600, from wood (n.).

waxwing.x: oscine passerine bird, 1817, from wax (n.) + wing (n.). So called for the appendages at the tips of its feathers which look like red sealing-wax.

wheeled.x: "having a wheel or wheels" of a certain description, c. 1600, from wheel (n.).

whipping.x:
1560s, "a beating with a whip," verbal noun from whip (v.). As "a defeat," 1835, American English colloquial.
Also as a present-participle adjective (1540s); hence whipping post (c. 1600), set up in a public place for offenders to be tied to and whipped; whipping boy (1640s), flogged in place of an erring but privileged pupil; whipping block (by 1810, in an account of criminal punishment in Russia).

worrying.x: 1826, "teasing, troubling, harassing; distressing to the mind or spirits," present-participle adjective from worry (v.). Related: Worryingly.

wedded.x: "married, joined in wedlock," late 12c., past-participle adjective from wed (v.). Also "of or pertaining to matrimony."

weeding.x: "act of clearing weeds," late 14c., verbal noun from weed (v.). Old English had weodung. Weeding-hook is from c. 1500.

works.x:
Middle English werkes, from Old English, "(someone's) deeds, acts, or actions, the things one has done in life," often especially in theology "good deeds, acts performed in obedience to the law of God," plural of work (n.).
The meaning "operations pertinent to maintaining a large physical place" (private, religious, or municipal) is from late 14c. Meaning "place established for the manufacture or performance of industrial labor" (usually with qualifying adjective) is from late 15c.
To be in the works in the extended sense of "in the process of being done or made" is by 1973.

winged.x: "provided with wings; having wings (of a specified type)," late 14c., past-participle adjective from wing (v.). As "shot or disabled in the wing" by 1789.

winning.x: "thing gained, thing won;" verbal noun from win (v.). By c. 1300 as "property or land taken by armed force;" by early 14c. as "earnings for work, one's income;" by mid-14c. as "financial success, monetary gain," also in a bad sense, "usury, ill-gotten gain." Related: Winnings. The sense of "act of triumphing in battle or combat" is by mid-14c.

1590s, "successful in contending," present-participle adjective from win (v.). Also from 1590s as "attractive, charming," as in win friends, on the notion of "influence, gain over." Related: Winningly. Winningest is attested by 1804.

wanting.x: "that is absent or lacking," a 16c. formation replacing wantand (early 14c.), "deficient, lacking," present-participle adjective from want (v.). An earlier adjective was wantsum "in want" (late 12c., from the noun).

Weigela.x: shrub genus, 1846, from the name of German physician and botanist C.E. Weigel (1748-1831). Properly formed it would be Weigela.

washing.x: Old English wæscing "action of washing clothes," verbal noun from wash (v.). The intransitive sense of "action of cleansing by bathing in water" is by early 13c. The meaning "clothes washed at one time" is by 1854. Washing machine, originally hand-powered, later steam-powered, is attested from 1754.

weeds.x:
"garments," plural of archaic weed "garment, article of clothing," especially an outer garment," hence weeds "clothes." This is from Middle English wede, from Old English wæd, wæde "robe, dress, apparel, garment, clothing."
This is reconstructed to be from Proto-Germanic *wed- (source also of Old Saxon wadi, Old Frisian wede "garment," Old Norse vað "cloth, texture," Old High German wat "garment"), which is of uncertain origin; according to Watkins probably from PIE *wedh-, extended form of root *au- (3) "to weave."
Archaic since early 19c. (now surviving, if at all, in widow's weeds "mourning clothes," which is attested from early 15c.), but very common in Middle English, which also had holiday weeds "festive garments;" in one weed "dressed alike;" under weeds "in disguise;" ironweeds "armor." Old Frisian cognate wede also was a unit of currency (value about 12 pence), preserving the early use of cloth as currency.

whistling.x: "action of producing a shrill note with the lips; action of playing a pipe;" Old English hwistlung, verbal noun from hwistlian (see whistle (v.)).

wallydraggle.x: "youngest of a family; bird in the nest; 'any feeble, ill-grown creature' " [Century Dictionary], 1817, earlier wallydrag (c, 1500), Scottish, of unknown origin.

wired.x:
Old English wired "made of wire," past-participle adjective from wire (v.).
It is attested by early 15c. as "pinned by or stiffened by wires." The meaning "nervous, jittery" is by 1970s; earlier (1959, perhaps early 1950s) "using narcotic drugs, addicted to drugs." By 1962 as "outfitted with a computer device."

weaving.x: "craft of producing fabric by interlacing threads on a loom," Old English wefung, verbal noun from weave (v.).

webbing.x: early 14c., "act or process of weaving," verbal noun from web (v.) or from Old English webbung "a weaving." As "wide, strong band of woven material" from 1794.

whaling.x: "whale-fishing" as a business, 1716, verbal noun from whale (v.1). Earlier were whale-fishing (1570s); whale-hunting (1610s).

wasted.x: late 14c., "enfeebled," past-participle adjective from waste (v.). The slang meaning "intoxicated" is from 1950s.

working.x:
late 14c., werking, of persons, "active, busy, occupied," present-participle adjective from work (v.). From 1620s as "engaged in physical toil or manual labor as a means of livelihood," especially for an employer.
In reference to a majority, "sufficient to secure passage of legislation," by 1858. Of a theory, etc., "providing a basis on which to work," by 1849.
Working class, collectively "those who earn by manual labor," is attested from 1757 as a noun, by 1839 as an adjective; working man "laboring man" is by 1650s. Working woman is attested by 1690s (earlier in Latin-English dictionaries such as Rider's and Thomas, 1590s, translating operaria). Working mother is by 1880. Working girl is by 1913; as a euphemism for "prostitute" by 1970. Working-day is from late 15c..
c. 1300, werking, "performance of work, labor," verbal noun from work (v.). Old English had wyrcung.

wonted.x:
"accustomed, made or having become usual," c. 1400, past-participle adjective formation from wont (adj.), older than wont (v.).
An unconscious double adjective, perhaps by confusion with wanted. Older was Middle English iwoned "accustomed, in the habit of," from Old English gewunod, past participle of gewunian.

weeping.x:
"that weeps; accompanied by tears," late Old English, present-participle adjective from weep (v.). Related: Weepingly.
Used of various trees whose branches arch downward and suggest drooping, such as weeping elm (c. 1600); weeping cherry (1824). Weeping willow (French saule pleureur, German trauerweide), introduced in England from the region of the Euphrates, is recorded by 1728 in Batty Langley's "New Principles of Gardening," which notes "the weeping or mourning Willow that was brought from Babylon, and now in great Plenty and Perfection in England. Particularly, in the Gardens of the late Thomas Vernon Esq., at his seat of Twickenham Park in Middlesex."
It replaced the cypress as a funerary emblem. There are also weeping ash, birch, oak.
"wailing, lamentation," c. 1200, verbal noun from weep (v.). Weep (n.) as "fit or bout of weeping" is attested by 1836.

witching.x: "display of supernatural or diabolical power," c. 1200, wicching, verbal noun from witch (v.). Old English had wiccung.

wertfrei.x: in sciences, etc., "neutrality in regard to value judgements; free from prevailing prejudices and passions," 1908, from German (by 1896), from wert "value" (see worth (adj.)) + frei "free," from Proto-Germanic *friaz "beloved; not in bondage" (reconstructed in Watkins to be from suffixed form of PIE root *pri- "to love"). Related: Wertfreiheit.

walking.x:
c. 1400, "going at a walk, not standing still," present-participle adjective from walk (v.). Walking distance is by 1817.
Walking sickness, one in which the sufferer is able to get about and is not bed-ridden, is from 1846. In Middle English medical writing walking was used of pathological conditions that appear to move about the body (late 14c.).
Walking wounded is recorded from 1917. Walking papers, colloquial for "dismissal," is by 1825. Walking bass, broken chords or scales played up and down, is attested from 1939 in jazz slang.
Walking stick "small staff for assistance in walking" is recorded from 1570s, often as a fashion accessory; the slender-bodied North American insect is so called by 1760, for its shape (colloquially stick-bug, by 1870).

waxhouse.x: also wax-house, late 14c., "beehive," also "place where candles are made," from wax (n.) + house (n.).

wanted.x:
1690s, "lacking;" 1812, "sought by the police;" past-participle adjective from want (v.). Wanted poster, showing persons sought by authorities (often advertising a reward for information or arrest), is attested by 1945.
As a noun, "persons or things wanted" (especially those advertised for or sought by police) is by 1793.

welcoming.x: from c. 1300 as a noun, "action of greeting kindly." By 1650s as an adjective, "that welcomes;" both from welcome (v.). Related: Welcomingly; welcomingness.

Wiffle.x: hollow, perforated plastic ball, registered trademark name (The Wiffle Ball Inc., Shelton, Connecticut, U.S.), claiming use from 1954. According to the company, designed in 1953 by David N. Mullany "in response to a lack of field space and numerous broken windows by his baseball-playing son," the name based on whiff (q.v.), baseball slang for a missed swing.

ways.x: "moral habits of life," Old English, plural of way (n.).

wadding.x: "stuffing, wads collectively," 1620s, verbal noun from wad (v.). Originally especially in gunnery; the sense of "cotton or wool used to line articles of dress" is by 1724.

wrapping.x: late 14c., "something used for rolling or folding together or enveloping;" mid-15c., "action of wrapping;" verbal noun from wrap (v.). Wrapping-paper is attested by 1715.

westerlies.x: "westerly winds," prevailing in certain latitudes, 1876, from westerly (adv.) "in a westerly direction."

whosis.x: 1923, short for who is this; whosit (who is it) is attested by 1948.

wakening.x: c. 1400, "a rousing from sleep," verbal noun from waken (v.).

wording.x: "choice of words, style or manner in which something is expressed," apparently coined in this sense by Milton in "Eikonoklastes" (1649). Verbal noun from word (v.). Earlier in now-obsolete sense of "utterance, speaking, talking" (c. 1600).

writing.x:
Old English writing "action or process of forming letters, the recording of words or sounds in significant characters," verbal noun from write (v.).
It is attested from c. 1200 as "text; body of poetry, narrative, etc. in written form; written material." From c. 1300 as "a particular text;" mid-14c. as "act of composing a written text."
It is by late 14c. as "craft of writing;" also "one's own handwriting or penmanship." Also late 14c. in the broad sense of "system of human intercommunication by means of conventional visible marks." Also late 14c. as "act of sending a letter; a letter, message."
The office writing-desk, sloped and with drawers, pigeon-holes, etc., is from 1610s; the library's open writing-table is from mid-15c. Writing-paper, sized and with a smooth surface for writing, is by late 15c.

weathered.x: 1789, of stone, etc., "discolored or deteriorated by exposure to weather," past-participle adjective from weather (v.1). Sometimes also of persons, "seasoned by exposure to weather."

worsted.x: woolen fabric made from twisted yarn, late 13c., from Worstead (Old English Wurðestede), town in Norfolk where the cloth originally was made. It is from worth "estate, manor" (see -worth) + stede "place" (see stead (n.)).

wondering.x: "expression of admiration or amazement," Old English wundrung, verbal noun; see wonder (v.).

weeded.x: 1766, "free from weeds," past-participle adjective from weed (v.) "clear ground of weeds." By 1818 as "full of or covered with weeds," from weed (n.) perhaps on model of seeded, planted, etc. By 1895, of a woman, "dressed in widow's weeds," from weeds.

whispering.x: "act or sound of a whisper; whispered talk; a speaking covertly;" from Old English hwisprung, verbal noun from hwisprian (see whisper (v.)). In reference to any soft, rustling sound resembling whispered speech, by c. 1600.

weanling.x: "child or young animal newly weaned," 1530s, from wean + -ling.

webbed.x: mid-15c., "covered with or as with a web" (in reference to a white film on the eye), past-participle adjective from web (v.).

Waring.x: brand name of a type of food blender, 1944, manufactured by Waring Products Corp., N.Y., U.S.

waiting.x:
"watching, looking, observation; an ambush," late Old English, verbal noun from wait (v.). From late 14c. as "service, attendance."
Waiting room is attested from 1680s. Waiting list is recorded from 1841; the verb wait-list "to put (someone) on a waiting list" is recorded from 1960. Waiting time is by 1962, originally in reference to computers. Waiting game is recorded from 1835, originally in horse-racing.
 When speed, not stoutness, is the best of a horse, quite a contrary system is practised.
