With such a horse, the jockey plays a waiting game; that is, he carefully nurses him through the race, so as not to distress him by overpacing him; as the finish approaches, he creeps up to his horses by degrees, but does not quit them to go in front till he sees that the pace has made them "safe," — when he lets loose and wins. [James Christie Whyte, "History of the British Turf," London, 1840]

welling.x: "an outpouring," c. 1400, verbal noun from well (v.).

winding.x: "curving, spiral; full of bends and turns," late 14c., present-participle adjective from wind (v.1). From 1520s as" that follows a sinuous course." Related: Windingly.

waning.x: Old English wanunge, wonunge, present participle of wanian (see wane).

Wankel.x: type of rotary internal combustion engine, 1961, from name of German engineer Felix Wankel (1902-1988).

Warfarin.x: anti-coagulant drug, 1950, from WARF, acronym from Wisconsin Alumni Research Foundation + -arin, from Coumarin. The organization describes itself as "an independent, nonprofit foundation chartered to support research at the U[niversity of] W[isconsin]-Madison and the designated technology transfer organization for the university."

withholding.x: late 14c., "the exercising of restraint, refusal to give (something) up, that which is retained," verbal noun from withhold (v.).

Windows.x: computer operating system by Microsoft, introduced in 1985, modified thereafter; it was dominant by c. 1995. Window (n.) in computing for the screen of a VDU regarded as a display space is by 1966; as a viewport by 1974.

willowy.x: "flexible and graceful," 1791, from willow + -y (2). Earlier "bordered or shaded by willows" (1751). Willowish is older (1650s) but in reference to the color of willow leaves. Related: Willowiness.

waistline.x: also waist-line, "line following the contours of the waist; a person's waist with reference to size;" 1867, from waist + line (n.).

wrathful.x: mid-13c., of words, "full of anger;" c. 1300, of persons, "angry;" of God, "righteously irate;" from wrath (n.) + -ful. Related: Wrathfully; wrathfulness. Wrathless is attested from mid-14c.

war-cry.x: "cry or phrase used in battle by a body of troops" for recognition or encouragement, by 1748; see war (n.) + cry (n.). Figurative use by 1836. War-whoop "yell of a particular intonation used as signal for attack and to strike terror in foes," is by 1739 in reference to native peoples of North America.

war-path.x: also warpath, "path followed by an expedition seeking battle," 1775, originally in reference to North American native peoples, as are war-whoop (1761; compare war-cry); war-paint (1826); and war-dance (1757), done before an expedition for battle. All with figurative extensions. See war (n.) + path (n.).

war-song.x: "song or chant raised by warriors about to seek battle; song praising military deeds;" 1757 (Burns), from war (n.) + song (n.).

Wardour-street.x:
"affected pseudo-archaic diction of historical novels," 1888, from street in London lined with shops selling imitation-antique furniture.
 This is not literary English of any date; this is Wardour-Street Early English — a perfectly modern article with a sham appearance of the real antique about it. [A. Ballantyne, "Wardour-Street English," Longman's Magazine, October 1888]

wart-hog.x: type of swine, so called from the excrescences on the face, 1840, from wart + hog (n.)."They are without exception the ugliest of mammals" [Century Dictionary].

wash-basket.x: also washbasket, circular shallow basket suitable for carrying clothes, 1851, from wash (n.) + basket (n.). Washing-basket is by 1947.

wash-cloth.x: also washcloth, "small piece of cloth used in washing the person, face, dishes," 1861, from wash (v.) + cloth (n.).

wash-house.x: "outbuilding, often fitted with boilers, tubs, etc., for washing clothes," 1570s, from wash (n.) + house (n.).

wash-room.x: also washroom, "room equipped for washing oneself, lavatory," 1806, from wash (v.) + room (n.).

wash-stand.x: also washstand, "hand-washing stand, piece of furniture made to hold a basin and ewer," 1789, from wash (v.) + stand (n.).

wash-tub.x: "tub in which clothes are washed," c. 1600 (washing-tub is from mid-15c.), from wash (v.) + tub (n.). In reference to an improvised double-bass, by 1968.

wasp-waist.x:
"very slender waist of a person's figure," by 1830; wasp-waisted (adj.) in reference to this is by 1827 in accounts (and condemnations) of fashionable young women; wasp's waist is attested earlier (by 1822) in reference to a men's style popular among dandies. So called in reference to the narrow juncture of thorax and abdomen in the insect; see wasp (n.) + waist (n.).
An 1827 critic of "modern wives" who can work a "peanner" but not a spinning-wheel writes that he would give more for a "damsel that understands cooking and can knit her own stockings, than for half a score of pale faced, wasp waisted piano drummers." [Bowling Green (Ky.) Spirit of the Times, Nov. 3, 1827]
In reference to a fashionably trim man:
 Half of our men of fashion vote themselves all-accomplished, if they can waltz, quadrille, shew a wasp's waist, (but want his spirit to sting,) wear effeminate pink cravats, and look more effeminate than the women they would win the passing admiration of, and disgrace by ogling and nodding to, (etc.) [Brighton Magazine, February 1822]

watch-band.x: "band for a wrist-watch," by 1924, from watch (n.) in the "timepiece" sense + band (n.1).

watch-case.x: hinged case for an old-fashioned watch, 1680s, from watch (n.) in the "timepiece" sense + case (n.2).

watch-chain.x: "small chain used as a watch-guard," 1739, from watch (n.) in the "timepiece" sense + chain (n.).

watch-light.x: "night-light, light kept burning at night, as in a sick room," 1620s, from watch (n.) + light (n.).

watch-pocket.x: "small pocket in a garment for carrying a watch," 1831, from watch (n.) in the "timepiece" sense + pocket (n.).

water-clock.x: device for measuring time by the amount of water discharged from one vessel into another (see clepsydra); from water (n.1) + clock (n.1).

water-drop.x: "drop of water," also "teardrop," by 1590s, from water (n.1) + drop (n.).

water-moccasin.x: type of snake in the U.S. South, 1821, from water (n.1) + moccasin (q.v.). Especially a highly venomous species, but the name is applied without distinction to similar-looking harmless snakes.

water-pipe.x: late 14c., "conduit for water," from water (n.1) + pipe (n.1). The smoking sense, "hookah," is attested by 1824.

water-side.x: also waterside, "bank or edge of a body of water," c. 1300, from water (n.1) + side (n.).

water-ski.x: "one of a pair of short, broad attachments enabling the wearer to skim the surf when pulled by a motorboat," 1931, from water (n.1) + ski (n.). As a verb from 1953. Related: Water-skiing; water-skier.

water-table.x: "level of saturated ground," 1879, from water (n.1) + table (n.).

water-tower.x: "tower holding a reservoir of water," c. 1300, water-tour; see water (n.1) + tower (n.).

watering-hole.x: "hole or hollow where water collects," 1882 (earlier water-hole, 1670s; watering-place, mid-15c.), and where animals gather to drink. See watering + hole (n.). It is attested by 1965 in the figurative sense "place where people meet and socialize over drinks."

way-maker.x: late 15c., "one who makes or mends roads;" 1570s, "pathfinder, pioneer," from way (n.) + maker.

way-mark.x: also waymark, "object serving as a guide to travelers" (a finger-post, milestone, etc.), from way (n.) + mark (n.1).

way-post.x: also waypost, "guidepost, finger-post," 1773; see way (n.) + post (n.1).

way-worn.x: "weary or worn with traveling," 1777, from way (n.) + worn (adj.).

weather-boarding.x: "flat, thin boards lapping one another as an outside covering for a wooden building," originally as protection from weather, 1630s, from weather (n.) + board (n.1). Also sometimes used of the finish at the base of a wall.

weather-cast.x: also weathercast, "forecast of the weather," 1866, from weather (n.) + ending from forecast (n.).

weather-side.x: "side of a ship toward the weather," late 14c., from weather (n.) in the nautical sense + side (n.).

well-acquainted.x: 1728, "having good intimacy with or knowledge of," from well (adv.) + acquainted.

well-digger.x: "person who excavates wells," 1600s, from well (n.) + digger (n.).

well-head.x: also wellhead, mid-12c., "source of a natural well or spring-fed stream," from well (n.) + head (n.).

well-said.x: "apt," late 15c., from well (adv.) + said. Well-saying (n.) "eloquence" is attested from early 15c.

well-spent.x: of time, "passed properly and virtuously," 1530s, from well (adv.) + past participle of spend.

wh-.x:
consonant cluster, a respelling of Old English hw-, Northumbrian hu- attested from 11c., widespread in some places by 14c., but not the common form overall until after c. 1400. The cluster represents PIE *kw-; in German reduced to simple w-, in Scandinavian as hv-, kv-, or v-.
It also was added unetymologically to some borrowed words (whisk, whiskey) and some native words formerly spelled with simple w- or h- (whole, whore). In the 15c. flowering of its use it also threatened to change the spelling of hot, home and many more.
Proper pronunciation in modern educated English speech has been much in dispute. In Middle English also vh-, qv-, qwh-, hu-; in northern English 16c.-18c., sometimes altered to quh- (see Q) which perhaps indicated a guttural enunciation, as also perhaps in earlier Northumbrian use of ch- in the pronouns.

wheel-base.x: also wheelbase, "distance between the front and back wheels of a vehicle where they touch the surface," 1886, originally of locomotives and railroad cars, from wheel (n.) + base (n.).

whip-saw.x: also whipsaw, "saw with a thin, flexible blade" especially for carved work, mid-15c., whip-saue, from whip + saw (n.). As a verb from 1842, "cut with a whip-saw." The noun sense of "something disadvantageous both ways" is by 1873, hence as a verb "have or take advantage of coming and going." Related: Whip-sawed; whip-sawing.

whip-snake.x: used of various species, by 1774, so called for their long, flexible shape; see whip (n.) + snake (n.).

whip-stock.x: "stick or handle to which the lash of a whip is attached," 1520s, from whip (n.) + stock (n.1).

whirl-about.x: "anything that spins rapidly," 1590s, from the verbal phrase; see whirl (v.) + about (adv.).

white-tail.x: common type of North American deer, 1872, from white (adj.) + tail (n.), so called from the fur on the underside of the tail, visible as it flees. White-tailed is from 1832.

whore-house.x: "house of ill-fame, brothel," early 14c., from whore (n.) + house (n.). Sometimes translating Latin lupanaria. Obsolete from c. 1700, revived early 20c. in American English.

whore-monger.x: also whoremonger, 1520s, from whore (n.) + monger (n.). A Petrus Hurmonger is in the 1327 Leicestershire Lay Subsidy Rolls. Related: Whoremongering.

wimpy.x:
1967, from wimp (n.) + -y (2). Related: Wimpiness. Wimpish is from 1925:
 Wimpish little men with spectacles, men whose collars did not meet. [Sinclair Lewis, "Arrowsmith"]

wind-down.x: "conclusion," 1969, from the verbal phrase, attested by 1952 as "come to an end," probably an image from a wind-up watch; see wind (v.1) + down (adv.).

wind-rose.x: "table or diagram showing frequency of winds from different points," 1590s, from wind (n.1) + rose (n.1).

wind-sock.x: also windsock, "cloth cone hung at an airfield, etc., to indicate direction of the wind," 1922, from wind (n.1) + sock (n.1).

window-pane.x: "pane of glass set in a window," by 1783, from window (n.) + pane (n.).

wine-skin.x: also wineskin, "wine vessel made from the nearly complete skin of a goat, pig, etc.," by 1749, from wine (n.) + skin (n.).

wire-cutter.x: by 1875 as a tool, nippers for cutting wire; by 1922 in reference to details of soldiers sent out to cut enemy barbed-wire in World War I; see wire (n.) + cut (v.).

wire-puller.x:
by 1842 in the political sense, on the image of pulling the wires that work a puppet (wire (n.) in this sense is from c. 1600); the image itself in politics is older:
 The ministerial majority being thus reduced to five in a house of five hundred and eighty-three, Lord John Russell and Lord Melbourne respectively announce the breaking up of the administration, and the curtain falls on the first act of the political farce, to the infinite annoyance and surprise of the prime wire-puller in the puppet-show. [British and Foreign Review, vol. IX, July-October 1839]
Related: Wire-pulling.

wl-.x: an initial sound cluster in words in Old English and early Middle English; among the Old English words were wlanc "stately, splendid;" wlætung "nausea;" wlenc "pride, arrogance" (Middle English wlonk); wlite "brightness, beauty, splendor;" wlitig" radiant, physically beautiful (Middle English wliti).

wonder-struck.x: "astonished with admiration or surprise," 1590s, wonder-strook; see wonder (n.) + struck. Related: Wonder-stricken.

wonder-worker.x: "one who performs miracles or marvelous things," 1590s, from wonder (n.) + worker; translating Greek thaumatourgos. Wonderwork "prodigy, miracle, holy thing, wonderous act" is Old English wundorweorc. Compare thaumaturge.

wood-note.x: "wild or natural musical tone," as the thrush or nightingale, but most uses echo Milton's woodnotes wild (1632), a reference to the qualities in Shakespeare. See wood (n.) + note (n.).

wood-thrush.x: beautiful, tuneful bird of eastern U.S., by 1791, from wood (n.) + thrush (n.1).

wr-.x: common Germanic consonant combination, especially to start words implying twisting or distortion. Also retained in Dutch and Flemish; reduced to -r- in Old High German and Old Norse; represented by vr- in Danish and Swedish; still spelled -wr- in English, but the -w- ceased to be pronounced c. 1450-1700 except in dialects.

Warner.x:
surname, by late 12c. as Warnier, mid-14c., Warnyr, literally "warrener," from Middle English wareiner "keeper of a warren" (late 13c.), from Old North French warennier (Old French garenier). The keeping of warrens formerly was an important function (see warren (n.)).
As an agent-noun, warner in the sense of "one who or that which warns" is by 1560s (see warn (v.)), too late to be the source of the name. The Warner Bros. film studio was founded 1923 by Harry, Albert, Sam, and Jack Warner, whose surname had been anglicized after immigration to U.S.

Wendy.x: fem. given name, apparently coined by James M. Barrie ("Peter and Wendy," 1911); it first registers on the U.S. Social Security list of popular baby names in 1936 and was in the top 40 names for girls born in the U.S. from 1965 to 1976. Wendy house, "small play house for children," is by 1949, from Barrie's books.

Westminster.x:
name of an ancient abbey and church on the north bank of the Thames west of old London (see west + minster), rebuilt 11c. and serving as the home of the national government from c. 1200.
By metonymy as "Parliament," by 1807. By 1860 in reference to a pattern of chimes using four bells struck in different five-note sequences to mark the quarter hours.

Wagner.x:
surname of Germanic origin, also in English Waggener, Waggoner, Wagener, "maker or driver of wagons" (see wagon (n.)). The native equivalent surname is Wayne, Wainwright or in some cases Carter.
Wagnerian in reference to Richard Wagner (1813-1883), the celebrated German composer of music-dramas, is by 1855, in a (humorous) letter to the editor of "The Musical World," published Dec. 1:
 ... to say nothing of the endless arguments I could bring to the point, were I disposed to be prolix—which, your readers will do me the justice to admit, I never am, except on certain subjects, such as the Wagnerian heresy and the Music of the Future.

workflow.x: "sequence of processes through which a piece of work passes," also work-flow, by 1949, from work (n.) + flow (n.).

WAC.x: 1943, American English, acronym from Women's Army Corps, formed 1943.

WPA.x: 1936, initialism (acronym) from Works Progress Administration, U.S. agency established 1935.

wae.x: obsolete or dialectal Scottish form of woe. Related: Waeful, waeness, waesome.

wap.x:
"a hit, a sharp blow," also whap, late 14c., probably of imitative origin; compare whack, slap, etc. Also compare Middle English quappen "to struggle; to pound, throb" (intransitive), perhaps a variant, or an independent imitative verb, or from Middle Dutch quabbelen, etc.
The verb also is from late 14c., "to strike, knock, hit with a blow." In slang c. 1560-c. 1730 it meant "to copulate." Related: Wapped; wapping. Middle English writers also treated themselves to bewhap, outwapped.

wig.x: "artificial covering of hair for the head," 1670s, shortened form of periwig. The meaning "person who wears a wig (professionally)" is from 1828.

1826, "supply with a wig," from wig (n.). The earlier verb was bewig (see bewigged).
The meaning "behave hysterically" (usually with out) is attested by 1955, perhaps from notion in flip one's wig. The verb also had a colloquial sense of "scold severely," attested by 1829 (a wigging was "a scolding"), which might have contributed to this later sense.
Also compare dash my wig!, a former mild imprecation (1797), and wigs on the green (1856), Irish colloquial for "a fight or rumble" (in which wigs are likely to be detached from their wearers). Related: Wigged; wigging.

wog.x:
c. 1920, "a lower-class babu shipping clerk" [Partridge]; popularized in World War II British armed forces slang for "Arab," also "native of India" (especially as a servant or laborer), roughly equivalent to American gook.
Many acronym origins have been proposed, but none has been found satisfactory. Possibly shortened from golliwog, though Partridge Slang notes difficulties with this as the word was not originally applied to Black people. Nevertheless the derivation has been given as early as 1921.
 The King Edward's Horse called the Indian Cavalry ‘The Wogs’—which is the diminutive of ‘Golliwogs’,—a description that was very apt of these dark apparitions in khaki and tin-hats. [Lt. Col. Lionel James, The History of King Edward's Horse, 1921, describing events of 1918]
By 1962, Peter Shaffer's play The Public Eye uses the term in reference to a British man of Greek descent. Woggy, used to describe anyone of non-Anglo-Celtic origin, is attested by 1968, in Australia. By 1986 it is defined in Lexicographic Description of English as "a dark skinned foreigner."
Irvine Welsh's book Trainspotting (1993) references porridge wogs as a slur for Scottish people. The saying Wogs begin at Calais is by 1971, from the notion that all non-British people are wogs. Related: Wogland.

woo.x: "honorably seek the favor, affection, or love of," Middle English wouen, from Old English wogian "to woo, court, marry," of uncertain origin and with no known cognates; perhaps related to woh, wog- "bent, inclined," perhaps on the notion of "incline another toward oneself." Related: Wooed; wooing; wooer.

wop.x: derogatory for "Italian," 1912, American English slang, apparently from southern Italian dialect guappo "dandy, dude, stud," a greeting among male Neapolitans, said to be from Spanish guapo "bold, dandy," which is from Latin vappa "sour wine," also "worthless fellow;" related to vapidus (see vapid). Whether or not that is right, wop probably is not an acronym, and the usual story that it is one seems to date only to c. 1985.

wuz.x: by 1886, representing a casual or dialectal pronunciation of was.

Whig.x:
British political party, 1657, in part perhaps a disparaging use of whigg "a country bumpkin" (1640s); but mainly a shortened form of Whiggamore (1649) "one of the adherents of the Presbyterian cause in western Scotland who marched on Edinburgh in 1648 to oppose Charles I." Perhaps originally "a horse drover," from dialectal verb whig "to urge forward" + mare.
The name first was used in 1689 in reference to members of the British political party that opposed the Tories. In American history, "colonist who opposes Crown policies," from 1768. Later in the U.S. it was applied to opponents of Andrew Jackson (as early as 1825), and taken as the name of a political party (1834) that merged into the Republican Party in 1854-56.
 [I]n the spring of 1834 Jackson's opponents adopted the name Whig, traditional term for critics of executive usurpations. James Watson Webb, editor of the New York Courier and Enquirer, encouraged use of the name. [Henry] Clay gave it national currency in a speech on April 14, 1834, likening "the whigs of the present day" to those who had resisted George III, and by summer it was official. [Daniel Walker Howe, "What Hath God Wrought," 2007]
Whig historian is recorded from 1924. Whig history is "the tendency in many historians ... to emphasise certain principles of progress in the past and to produce a story which is the ratification if not the glorification of the present." [Herbert Butterfield, "The Whig Interpretation of History," 1931]

wack.x: "crazy person," by 1938, probably a back-formation from wacky. As an adjective in slang sense of "worthless, stupid," it is attested from late 1990s.

wadi.x: "channel of a watercourse that is dry except in the rainy season," 1839, from Arabic wadi "seasonal watercourse," prop. participle of wada "it flowed." It is the source of the Guadal- in Spanish river names.

wan-.x:
word-forming element of Germanic origin, frequent in Old English, still common in Middle English, still present in 18c. glossaries of Scottish and Northern English, now archaic except for wanton. Its force is negative and privative: "wanting, lacking, deficient," also "wrongly, badly; mistaken." It was used interchangeably with un- (1).
It is cognate with German wahn-, Dutch wan- (as in wanbestuur "misgovernment," wanluid "discordant sound"), Swedish and Danish van-, from Proto-Germanic *wano- "lacking" (see wane (v.); also compare wan (adj.)).

wang.x: "penis," 1933, slang, probably from whangdoodle, an earlier term for "gadget, thing for which the correct name is not known." Many such words (thingy, dingus, etc.) have been used in slang for "penis," not because the actual name was unknown, but because it was unmentionable. Another possibility is that the slang word is a variant of whang "large, thick slice" (1630s), which earlier was used in the sense of "thong" (1530s) and is itself a variant of thwang, an alternative form of thong (see thong). In Old English, wang meant "cheek, jaw," hence wangtoð "cheek-tooth, molar."

wank.x: "act of (male) masturbation," 1948 (Partridge), slang. As a verb by 1950. Related: Wanked; wanking. Compare wanker.

waul.x: "cry as a cat or infant, yowl, squall," 14c., also waw, probably partly imitative but sometimes said to be from Old English *wrag, *wrah "angry," a word of uncertain origin but itself somehow imitative. Also as a noun.

wavy.x: 1580s, "having a wavy appearance;" 1590s, "abounding in waves;" from wave (n.) + -y (2). Of movements, "forming wave-like curves," 1701. Earlier form was waui, "full of waves, billowy" (early 15c.). Related: Waviness.

weel.x: "deep pool, whirlpool," Middle English wel, from Old English wæl "whirlpool, eddy; pool; sea," cognate with West Frisian wiel, Old Low Frankish wal, Middle Dutch wael, German wehl, wehle.
"trap or snare for catching fish, crabs., etc.," probably originally of wicker, mid-13c., wele, a word of uncertain origin, probably from Old English or Old Norse. Obsolete or provincial.

weet.x: "to know" (archaic), 1540s, from Middle English weten, variant of witen "to know" (see wit (v.)).

wham.x: "a heavy blow," 1923, of echoic origin. As a verb, "strike violently," by 1925. As an intensive by 1924. Intensified wham-bam is by 1960 as "loud, violent;" as adverb or interjection (suggestively and followed by thank you ma'am) by 1971.

whew.x: exclamation of astonishment, etc., early 15c., quhewe, imitative of a whistling sound.

whey.x: the watery part of milk, Middle English whei, from Old English hwæg "whey," from Proto-Germanic *hwaja- (source also of Middle Dutch wey, Dutch wei), a word of unknown origin.

whir.x: c. 1400, whirren, Scottish, "fling, hurl" (arrows), "fly or dart with a whizzing sound, move in a noisy rush," probably from Old Norse hvirfla, frequentative of hverfa "to turn" (see wharf). Compare Danish hvirvle, Dutch wervelen, German wirbeln "to whirl." Related: Whirred; whirring.

whiz.x: "clever person," 1914, probably a special use of whiz "something remarkable" (1908), an extended sense of whizz; or perhaps a shortened and altered form of wizard. The noun phrase whiz kid is from 1930s, a take-off on a radio show's quiz kid.

whoa.x: 1620s, a cry to call attention from a distance, a variant of who. Obsolete in the original sense. As a command to stop a horse, it is attested from 1843, a variant of ho. As an expression of delight or surprise (1980s) it gradually superseded wow, which was popular 1960s.

whop.x: "to beat, strike with a heavy blow," mid-15c., of imitative origin. Compare Welsh chwap "a stroke," also of imitative origin; also see wap. Related: Whopped; whopping.

wich.x: "salt works, salt pit," also wych, from Old English wic, apparently a specialized use of the wic that means "dwelling place, town" (see wick (n.2)).

wimp.x: 1920 (George Ade, not attested again until 1960), perhaps a clipped form of whimper (cf whimp, 1540s), later perhaps influenced by J. Wellington Wimpy, comparatively unaggressive character in "Popeye" comics, who debuted in 1931. Wimp also formerly was slang for "female, young woman" (1923), of obscure origin. Also compare old slang wump "foolish or feeble person" (1908).
1986, with out (adv.), from wimp (n.). Related: Wimped; wimping.

wino.x: "habitual drunkard," especially if indigent and drinking cheap wine, 1915, from wine + slang suffix -o as in bucko, kiddo.

wiry.x: 1580s, "made of wire," from wire (n.) + -y (2). As "resembling or in the form of wire" from 1590s; of persons, "lean, sinewy, tough, and flexible," by 1808. Related: Wirily; wiriness.

wist.x:
"to know" (archaic), c. 1500, a spurious word from the past tense of wit (v.) "to know" improperly used as present indicative (in place of wists). It is cognate with German wusste, past tense of wissen "to know."
Had-I-wiste was used c. 1400-1550 in sense "regret for something done rashly or heedlessly;" see wist. Proverbial in expression Had-I-wiste cometh ever too late.
 Haddywyst comyth euer to late Whan lewyd woordis beth owte y-spronge. ["Commonplace book" in Trinity College, Cambridge, c. 1500]

wive.x: "to marry (a woman), take a spouse in marriage," usually of a man, Middle English wiven, from Old English wifian, from wif "woman" (see wife). Compare Middle Dutch wiven. The transitive sense of "provide with a wife" is attested from 1510s. Related: Wived; wiving. Wiving (n.) "act of taking a wife, state of being married" (of a man) is Old English wifung.

woad.x:
plant formerly much cultivated for the blue dye extracted from its fermented leaves, also the dye itself; Middle English wode, from Old English wad "woad," also the blue dye made from its leaves, from Proto-Germanic *waidīn, which is perhaps cognate with Latin vitrium "glass" (see vitreous). Boutkan considers it a substratum word. The dye with which the ancient Britons painted themselves blue, it has since been superseded commercially by indigo.
Germanic cognates include Danish vaid, Old Frisian wed, Middle Dutch wede, Dutch wede, Old High German weit, German Waid "woad." Middle English also had the word as waide, via Anglo-French or directly from the Old North French form. French guède, Italian guado are considered Germanic loan-words.

womb.x:
Middle English wombe, "human stomach as an organ of digestion," from Old English wamb, womb "belly, surface of the abdomen; bowels;" figuratively, "gluttony, hunger," also "uterus;" from Proto-Germanic *wambo, a word of unknown origin. The English word is obsolete in all senses but the last.
Germanic cognates include Old Norse vomb, Old Frisian wambe, Middle Dutch wamme, Dutch wam, Old High German wamba, German Wamme "belly, paunch," Gothic wamba "belly, womb," Old English umbor "child."
Also used of the uterus of the larger and better-known mammals. Extended late 14c. to a hollow or interior part that receives anything; also figurative of "seat of emotions, one's deepest self." Related: Wombful. Womby (mid-15c.) was "of the flesh, carnal." Fruit of (one's) womb "children" is by late 13c.

wone.x: obsolete verb, "dwell, abide; be accustomed," Middle English wonen, from Old English wonian "dwell, remain," cognate with German wohnen "reside," from Proto-Germanic *wunen "to be content, to rejoice," reconstructed in Watkins to be from PIE root *wen- (1) "to desire, strive for." The original meaning of the Germanic verbs would be "be content, rejoice." Compare wont (adj.).

wonk.x:
"overly studious person," 1962, earlier "effeminate male" (1954), American English student slang. Perhaps a shortening of British slang wonky "shaky, unreliable," or a variant of British slang wanker "masturbator."
It seems to have risen from Ivy League slang into currency late 1980s as a synonym for nerd, and as such was popularized 1993 during the presidency of Bill Clinton. Tom Wolfe (1988) described it as "an Eastern prep-school term referring to all those who do not have the 'honk' voice, i.e., all who are non-aristocratic."

wren.x: common, very small, brown migratory bird, Middle English wrenne, from Old English wrenna, metathesis variation of earlier werna, a Germanic word of uncertain origin. Compare Icelandic rindill, Old High German wrendo, wrendilo "wren." Active and sprightly, with a pleasant song, it features extensively in English folklore, often nicknamed Jenny, Katie, Kitty.

wuss.x:
by 1981 in U.S. college slang, perhaps abbreviated from wussy.
 Mike Damone: "You are a wuss: part wimp, and part pussy"
 ["Fast Times at Ridgemont High" script, 1982]

Weber.x: surname, attested from 1255; "one whose occupation is a weaver," literally "webber" (see web (n.1) + -er (1)); perhaps a variant of Weaver by influence of web. It also is the common German form of the surname. Also compare webster.

wacko.x: extended form of wack, by 1971. Also see -o.

wacky.x: "crazy, eccentric," by 1935, perhaps a variant of whacky (n.) "fool," late 19c. British slang; probably ultimately from whack (n.) "a blow, stroke," on the notion of being hit on the head too often.

wader.x: 1670s, "one who or that which wades," agent noun from wade (v.). It is attested by 1771 in reference to long-legged water-birds. Waders, "waterproof high boots worn by fishermen and sportsmen," is by 1841.

wahoo.x: type of large marine fish caught near Key West, 1884, a word of unknown origin. It earlier is attested as a name for certain North American trees or shrubs (by 1770), from distortions of native names; especially the "burning bush," from Dakota (Siouan) wahu, from wa- "arrow" + -hu "wood." In reference to the winged elm, it is from Muskogee vhahwv.

wally.x: term of admiration, Scottish, early 16c., a word of unknown origin. As a masc. proper name, a diminutive of Walter, and this might be the source of the teen slang term "unfashionable person" (1969).

washy.x: 1610s, "over-diluted," from wash (n.) + -y (2). The sense of "feeble, wanting strength or stamina" is from 1630s. Related: Washiness.

waxen.x: "made of wax, covered with wax," Old English wexen; see wax (n.) + -en (2).

weedy.x:
mid-15c., wedi, "overgrown with weeds," from weed (n.) + -y (2). By c. 1600 as "having the character of a weed." In old slang, in reference to horses, "not of good blood or strength, scraggy, worthless for breeding or racing," from 1800; hence, of persons, "thin and weakly" (1852).
Of women, "wearing weeds," by 1842, from weeds.

weeny.x: "tiny, very small," 1790, from wee (adj.) + ending as in teeny (from tiny). As a noun, "very young child," by 1844.

weepy.x: 1825, "exuding moisture, seepy," from weep + -y (2). By 1863 as "inclined to shed tears." Related: Weepily; weepiness. Weepie (n.) "sentimental film" is attested from 1928. Middle English had wepeli "mournful, tearful;" wepeful, both late 14c.

weism.x: "(too) frequent use of the pronoun 'we,' " 1800, from we + -ism. Compare wegotism.

welch.x: "refuse or avoid payment of money laid as a bet," by 1857, racing slang, probably a disparaging use of the national name Welsh (q.v.) or from a surname now otherwise forgotten. Related: Welched; welcher; welching.

whack.x:
"strike sharply, give a heavy blow to," 1719, colloquial, probably of imitative origin. The noun, "vigorous stroke, as with a stick" is from 1737. The word in out of whack (1885) is perhaps the slang meaning "share, just portion" (1785), which may be from the notion of the blow that divides, or the rap of the auctioneer's hammer.
To have (or take) a whack at something "make an attempt" is by 1820 (with have), 1845 (with take). Wack or whack "crazy person," 1938, is probably a back-formation from wacky, which probably comes from the blow-on-the-head verb. Related: Whacked; whacking. Whacked as "tired exhausted" is by 1919; whacked out "crazy," especially from drugs or drink, is by 1969.
Wack, whack in the slang sense of "unappealing; crazy," hence "worthless, stupid" is by 1986, apparently popularized by an anti-drug slogan crack is wack.

whang.x: 1530s, "thong, strap," especially if of leather, a variant of thwang, an alternative form of thong (see thong). By 1680s as "a big slice." As a verb by 1680s as "beat, flog, whack;" by 1743 as "cut in large portions."

wharf.x:
"supported platform or other structure of some size into a river or other body of water, where ships can tie up and load or unload;" late Old English hwearf "shore, bank where ships can tie up," earlier "dam, embankment," from Proto-Germanic *hwarfaz (source also of Middle Low German werf "mole, dam, wharf," German Werft "shipyard, dockyard"); related to Old English hwearfian "to turn," perhaps in a sense implying "busy activity."
This is reconstructed to be from PIE root *kwerp- "to turn, revolve" (source also of Old Norse hverfa "to turn round," German werben "to enlist, solicit, court, woo," Gothic hvairban "to wander," Greek karpos "wrist," Sanskrit surpam "winnowing fan").
Wharf rat is attested from 1812 in reference to the type of rat common on ships and docks, commonly the brown rat,
 considered with reference to its being in many places an imported animal, first naturalized in wharves after leaving the ship which brings it, or to the special size, ferocity, or other distinctive character it acquires under the favorable conditions of environment afforded by wharves, shipping, and storehouses. [Century Dictionary]
The extended sense "person who hangs around docks" is recorded from 1836.

wheal.x: "elongated mark made on the skin by a whip or blow," 1808, perhaps an alteration of wale, possibly by confusion with weal (n.2) "welt," and obsolete wheal "pimple, pustule" (mid-15c.), which is from Middle English whelen "become blistered," from Old English verb hwelian "to form pus, bring to a head." Middle English also had related whele, in pathology, "a raised sore" (late 14c.), but the modern word is a fresh formation.

whisk.x:
late 14c., "quick stroke, sweeping movement," probably from Old Norse visk "wisp of hay, something to sweep with," from Proto-Germanic *wisk- "move quickly," from PIE root *weis- "to turn, twist." The unetymological wh- is attested from 1570s.
The meaning "small implement for beating or agitating eggs, cream, etc." is recorded by 1660s.
Germanic cognates include Danish visk "broom," Middle Dutch wisch, Dutch wis, Old High German wisc, German wisch "wisp, brush." The PIE root also is reconstructed to be the source of Sanskrit veskah "noose," Czech vechet "a wisp of straw," Old English wiscian "to plait," weoxian "to clean" with a whisk or brush.

late 15c., quhisk, "move with a rapid sweeping motion" (intransitive), from a Scandinavian source (compare Danish viske "to wipe, rub, sponge," Norwegian, Swedish viska "wipe," also "wag the tail"), from the source of whisk (n.).
The transitive sense of "move (something) with a light, sweeping motion" is attested from 1510s; the meaning "brush or sweep (something) lightly over a surface" is from 1620s. Related: Whisked; whisking.

whist.x:
card game for four, 1660s, alteration of whisk, name of a kind of card game, alluded to as early as 1520s, perhaps so called from the notion of "whisking" up cards after each trick, and thus from whisk (v.).
It was then perhaps altered by influence of whist, also whish, the exclamation to suggest silence to one nearby (which is attested by late 14c.), but in most sources this is not considered the direct source of the card-game name, nor is "silence" considered the etymological sense of it. "The rule of silence, so far as it exists, is appar[ently] founded, however, in part on the false etymology." [Century Dictionary]

whizz.x: also whiz, "make or move with a humming, hissing sound," as an arrow through the air, 1540s, of imitative origin. Meaning "to urinate" is from 1929. Related: Whizzed; whizzing. The noun is recorded from 1610s. Whizzer "something extraordinary" is from 1888.

whomp.x: 1926, echoic of the sound of a heavy blow or something falling heavily.
"hit hard, defeat decisively;" 1952, from whomp (n.). Related: Whomped; whomping.

whoop.x:
mid-14c., houpen, whopen, "shout with a loud, excited voice," partly imitative, partly from Old French huper, houper "to cry out, shout," also imitative. It is attested as an interjection from at least mid-15c. The spelling with wh- is from mid-15c. The noun, "loud call, hooting cry," is Middle English houp.
Phrase whoop it up "create a disturbance" is recorded from 1881.
Whooping cough (1739), the acute, contagious childhood disease so called for its peculiar cough, is now the prevalent spelling of hooping cough; whooping crane, in reference to a large, white North American bird so called for its cry, is recorded from 1791.

whoso.x: "whoever, whatever person," late Old English, from who + so. Related: Whosoever (early 13c.).

whump.x: "make a dull, thudding sound," 1897, of imitative origin. Also wumph (1913). Related: Whumped; whumping. The noun is recorded from 1915.

wi-fi.x: 1999, apparently from wireless; the second element perhaps suggested by hi-fi.

wilco.x: 1945, in two-way radio slang, abbreviation and conflation of will comply.

windy.x: Middle English windi, from wind (n.1) and from Old English windig, of seasons, "exposed to wind;" see wind (n.1) + -y (2). The meaning "affected by flatulence" is in late Old English; of food, "causing flatulence," late 14c. Related: Windily; windiness. Chicago has been the Windy City at least since 1885.

wiper.x: 1550s, "workman employed in drying something;" 1580s, "a cloth for wiping;" agent noun wipe (v.). From 1929 as short for windshield-wiper.

witty.x:
Middle English witti, from Old English wittig "clever, wise, sagacious; in one's right mind;" see wit (n.) "intellect" + -y (2).
Original senses now all obsolete. By early 15c. as "crafty, cunning." The meaning "possessing sparkling wit" is recorded from 1580s. Related: Wittily; wittiness. Middle English had all-witty "omniscient" (c. 1400).

wryly.x: "in a wry, distorted, or awkward manner," 1570s, from wry (adj.) + -ly (2).

wussy.x: 1960s, probably an alteration of pussy (n.2). "Dictionary of American Slang" suggests shortened from hypothetical pussy-wussy, reduplicated form of pussy (n.1).

Wahabi.x: also Wahabee, 1807, follower of Islamic fundamentalist Abd-el-Wahhab (1691-1787); they are so called from his name, with Arabic genitive suffix -i. Related: Wahabiism; Wahabism; Wahabist; Wahabite.

Warsaw.x: Polish capital, Polish Warszawa, a name of unknown origin. Related: Varsovian. The Warsaw Pact "Cold War Eastern Bloc military alliance" is from the Treaty of Warsaw, signed there May 14, 1955. Signatories were the Soviet Union, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Albania.

Watusi.x: ethnic group in Rwanda and Burundi (also called Tutsi), 1899. As the name of a popular U.S. dance, attested from 1964.

whoot.x: a variant of hoot (v.) attested by c. 1400.

waiter.x: late 14c., "watchman, spy" (senses now obsolete); late 15c., "attendant at a meal, servant who waits at tables;" agent noun from wait (v.). In the surviving sense, originally of household servants; in reference to table attendants at inns, eating houses, etc., it is attested from 1660s. Also from 1650s as "one who abides in expectation" of some event or time.

walrus.x:
"very large pinniped carnivorous mammal" (the males are noted for their enormous tusk-like canine teeth), 1650s, from Dutch walrus, which was probably a folk-etymology alteration (by influence of Dutch walvis "whale" and ros "horse") of a Scandinavian word, such as Old Norse rosmhvalr "walrus," hrosshvalr "a kind of whale," or rostungr "walrus."
Old English had horschwæl, and later morse, from Lapp morsa or Finnish mursu, which ultimately might be the source, much garbled, of the first element in Old Norse rosmhvalr.
In reference to a type of large, overgrown mustache, by 1888.

wanker.x: 1940s, "masturbator," British slang, from wank "to masturbate," of unknown origin. General sense of "contemptible person" is attested from 1972. Compare sense evolution of jerk (n.).

warmer.x: "one who or that which makes warm or warmer," 1590s, agent noun from warm (v.). Compare bench-warmer; leg-warmer.

warmly.x: 1520s, of feelings, "fervently, earnestly;" 1590s in reference to temperature, "in a warm manner, so as to be warm;" from warm (adj.) + -ly (2).

wasabi.x: horseradish-like herb root used in Japanese cooking, 1903, from Japanese.

wassup.x: slang form of common greeting what's up?, very popular in 2000.

weeder.x: mid-14c., "person who removes weeds;" by early 15c. as "tool or implement for removing weeds;" agent noun from weed (v.).

weenie.x:
"frankfurter," 1906, with slang sense of "penis" following soon after, from German wienerwurst "Vienna sausage" (see wiener).
The meaning "ineffectual person, effeminate young man" is slang from 1963; pejorative sense via penis shape, or perhaps from or bolstered by weeny "very small."

weirdo.x:
"strange person," by 1950, from weird + -o. As an adjective by 1962. Compare earlier Scottish weirdie "odd, unconventional person" (by 1887).
 [Marlon] Brando said Tallulah Bankhead—with whom he performed in "An Eagle Has Two Heads"—considered him a "weird-o." [Press of Atlantic City (N.J.), May 18, 1950]
Also a surname in New Jersey.

wheezy.x: 1818, "characterized by wheezing," from wheeze + -y (2). Related: Wheezily; wheeziness.

whimsy.x: "capricious notion or fancy," c. 1600, probably related to whimwham, and compare whim (n.), its later form.

whiney.x: also whiny, "characterized by or disposed to whining," by 1854, from whine (n.) + -y (2). Related: Whininess.

whiten.x:
c. 1300, whitenen, "to make white," from white (adj.) + -en (1).
By c. 1400 as "purify spiritually." By early 15c. as "make (one's face) white by cosmetics." The intransitive sense of "become white" is attested from 1630s. The earlier verb was simply white (v.), now only archaic or Biblical. Related: Whitened; whitening; whitener.

whitey.x:
"'white' person, person of European descent," 1828, also whity, from white (adj.) + -y (2) and -y (3). Earlier as an adjective, and Whitey-brown was a 19c. descriptive color name, used to describe, among other things, mulatto skin.
 Negro troops doing provost duty in Norfolk; keeping the white people in order. On a visit to Norfolk one can see white Southerners, arrested for sundry misdemeanors, working on the public streets, under negro guards. ... It is quite a change to see, in Norfolk, negroes forcing white men to work, at the point of the bayonet; calling out to them: "No loaf'n dar!" "Move quicker, Sah!" "Hurry up dar, Old Whitey!" and similar orders. Tables turned! [diary of Lieut. S. Millett Thompson, 13th New Hampshire Volunteer regiment, U.S. Army, Jan. 25, 1864; diary published 1888 by Houghton, Mifflin & Co.]

wholly.x: mid-14c., holli, "completely, entirely; in a body, together; in full, fully; from whole (adj.) + -ly (2), or a modification of unrecorded Old English *hallice. By late 14c. as "wholeheartedly."

whoosh.x: "make a sound like something rushing through the air," 1856, of imitative origin. Related: Whooshed; whooshing. As a noun from 1880; as an interjection by 1899.

wibble.x: 1871, from wibble-wobble (1847), symbolizing alternating movement, a colloquial reduplication of wobble (v.).

wifely.x: Middle English wifli, late 14c., "pertaining to or befitting a wife," from wife (n.) + -ly (1). Old English wiflic meant "womanly, pertaining to a woman." Wifelike "resembling or pertaining to a wife" is attested by 1590s.

wiggly.x: "characterized by successive or frequent wiggling," 1878, from wiggle (n.) + -y (2).

willya.x: representing the contracted pronunciation of will you?, often as an emphatic after a command or request, attested by 1941.

wintry.x: "of, pertaining to, or occurring in winter," 1580s, from winter (n.) + -y (2). Old English had wintrig; also winterlic, Middle English winterly, "resembling or characteristic of winter," "but the modern word appears to be a new formation" [Barnhart]. Similar formation in German wintericht. Middle English wintred (late 12c.) could mean "aged" or "wintry."

wisely.x: "with wisdom, discretion, cunning, or skill," Middle English wiseli, from Old English wislice; see wise (adj.) + -ly (2).

withal.x: "in addition, with all, along with the rest," late 14c., from Middle English with alle (c. 1200), superseding Old English mid ealle "wholly." See with + all. As an emphatic preposition, early 14c., used after the object at the end of a sentence or clause.

woeful.x: early 14c., woful, "afflicted by sorrow, full of grief," from woe + -ful. The weakened sense of "very bad, paltry," is recorded by 1610s. Related: Woefully; woefulness.

wonton.x: also won ton, 1948, said to be from Cantonese wan t'an, Mandarin hun tun "stuffed dumpling."

worsen.x:
mid-13c., wersnen "make (someone's condition) worse," also "grow worse" (of a wound, etc.), from worse (adj.) + -en (1).
The intransitive sense of "get worse, become worse off" (formerly in worse (v.)), was notably revived in literary use c. 1800-1830 by Southey and his followers.
 After being good Old English, it long had no vogue but provincial. It is not surprising that those who write much should, if they know the word, now and then feel deteriorate to be weak in comparison. [Fitzedward Hall, "Modern English," 1873]
Related: Worsened; worsening.

worser.x:
a double comparative, "due to the fact that worse (like less) is not obviously a compar. form" [Century Dictionary]; see worse + -er (2).
Attested from late 15c. and common 16c.-17c. Modern use can be literary archaism or humorous. Noun worsers "(one's) inferiors" is from 1580s. Related: Worserer (1752).

woulda.x: representing a casual pronunciation of would have (or incorrect would of); attested in print by 1913.

Wallach.x: also Walach, one of a Rumanian people, 1786, from German Wallache, from Old Church Slavonic Vlachu, from Old High German wahl "foreigner, one speaking a foreign language," a name applied by ancient Germanic peoples on one side to their Slavic neighbors and on the other to the Celts of Britain (see Vlach and compare Welsh). Related: Wallachia, former Danubian principality; Wallachian.

Werther.x:
love-lorn hero of Goethe's "Die Leiden des jungen Werthers" ("The Sorrows of Young Werther"), popular and influential short novel published in 1774 (translated into English by 1779). His name was used as a type of morbid sentimentality among young Germans. Related: Wertherian; Wertherism.
The character name is probably taken from the town of Werther in modern North Rhine-Westphalia, said to be from Old High German weridhari, "guardian of the weir." The hard candy Werther's Originals started being marketed in America with the name in 1981, from the original German Werthers Echte, named for the town where they were first manufactured.

Wilhelm.x: masc. proper name, German form of William (q.v.). Fem. form is Wilhelmina. Wilhelmine (adj.) is "pertaining to the reign of Wilhelm II," emperor of Germany 1888-1918. Berlin's Wilhelmstrasse was the pre-1945 headquarters of the German foreign office, hence used metonymically for "German foreign policy" (compare Quai d'Orsay).

wackjob.x: also whackjob, wack job, 1979, "crazy person." From wack (n.) + job (n.) in the broad sense "example of." Perhaps on model of earlier nut job (1972) with same meaning.

wagoner.x: also waggoner, "one who leads or drives a wagon," 1540s, perhaps a loan-translation of Dutch waghenauer; see wagon + -er (1). The military wagon-master is attested from 1640s.

waifish.x: "resembling a waif," 1870, from waif + -ish. Related: Waifishly; waifishness.

wake-up.x:
"that which brings one to alertness or out of sleep," 1965, from verbal phrase wake up, which is attested by 1530s as "rouse (someone) to action, excite" and by 1763 as "rouse (someone) from sleep." It is attested by 1837 intransitively as "cease to sleep," but the up there is redundant (or intensive).
The phrase wake-up call is attested from 1968, originally a call one received from the hotel desk in the morning. Verbal phrase wake up is from 1530s; earlier the adverb was out (late 14c.)
To wake up (a place) "disturb the peace of, make noisy and busy" is by 1848. During the 1960s the noun was often in reference to a shot of heroin in the morning.

wakeful.x: c. 1400, "diligent, unceasing in attention," from wake (n.2) + -ful. By 1620s as "insomniac." Related: Wakefully; wakefulness.

walk-in.x: 1928, "without appointment," from the verbal phrase, from walk (v.) + in (adv.). As "large enough to walk into" (in reference to storage space) by 1943; as a noun, "walk-in closet," by 1946. In reference to rooms, "entered from another room rather than via a passage," by 1967.

walk-on.x:
"minor non-speaking role," 1902, theatrical slang, from the verbal phrase walk on, attested in theater jargon by 1897 as "appear in crowd scenes;" see walk (v.) + on (adv.).
In reference to an actor who has such a part, it is attested from 1946. In reference to an athlete without status seeking to join a sports team, by 1974.

walk-up.x: in reference to an apartment not accessible by elevator, 1909, from the verbal phrase; see walk (v.) + up (adv.). As a noun from 1920 in reference to such an apartment.

walkway.x: "pedestrian passageway," 1865, American English, from walk (v.) + way (n.).

wallaby.x: also wallabee, kind of small kangaroo, 1826, from native Australian wolaba.

walleye.x: type of fish (pike-perch), 1876, American English, said to be so-called from the positioning of the eyes (compare wall-eyed).

wanhope.x: "hopelessness, despair of salvation" as a theological sin (insufficient faith in God's mercy), late 13c.; see wan- + hope (n.). By c. 1300 also as "lack of confidence in oneself;" among the Elizabethans in a weakened sense of "faint hope" (1550s) as if from wan (adj.).

wannabe.x: also wanna-be, 1981, originally American English surfer slang, from casual pronunciation of want to be; popularized c. 1984 in reference to female fans of pop singer Madonna. Compare wanna.

warhead.x: also war-head, 1898, "explosive part of a torpedo," from war (n.) + head (n.). Later transferred to the explosive tip of any missile (by 1944).

warlike.x: early 15c., "naturally disposed to warfare, fond of war," from war (n.) + like (adj.). An earlier adjective in the same sense was fighti "fighty" (mid-13c.). By 1560s as "of or pertaining to war, befitting a soldier."

warlord.x: also war-lord, "military commander," 1856, from war (n.) + lord (n.). Often a translation of German Kriegsherr or Chinese junfa.

warship.x: also war-ship, "ship built or fitted for use in war," 1530s, from war (n.) + ship (n.).

watcher.x: late 14c., waccher, "guard, watchman" (early 13c. as a surname), agent noun from watch (v.). By 1570s as "one who observes." In combinations with a noun, indicating one studiously interested in it, by 1887 (clock-watcher).

way-out.x:
1868, "far off," from the verbal phrase; from way (adv.), short for away, + out (adv.). The sense of "original, bold," is jazz slang from 1940s, probably suggesting "far off" from what is conventional or expected.
Way out (n.) "means of exit" is by 1926, from way (n.).

wayside.x: also way-side, "side of the road, edge of a path," c. 1400, from way (n.) + side (n.). To fall by the wayside is from Luke viii.5.

webwork.x: also web-work, Old English webweorc, "weaving;" see web (n.1) + work (n.).

wetness.x: Middle English wetnesse, "moisture, dampness," from Old English wetnise; see wet (adj.) + -ness.

what-if.x: 1973 as an adjective, 1974 as a noun, in speculations as to what might have been had circumstances or fate been different, from the interrogative phrase; see what + if.

whatnot.x:
also what-not, 1530s, "anything," from what + not. Elliptical for what may I not say, implying "everything else," and according to the scrupulous better left as two words in this sense.
As the name of a furniture item, attested by 1808, so called for the sort of objects it is meant to hold, the plural whatnots being also used "confusedly" [OED, 1989] for "miscellaneous things, bric-a-brac."
What-all as colloquial for "various other things" is by 1702; muchel-what (pron.) "sundry things" is from late 14c.

wheaten.x: "made of wheat, pertaining to wheat," Middle English wheten, from Old English hwæten; see wheat + -en (2). In reference to color resembling wheat, by 1943.

whereat.x: mid-13c., "to what purpose;" early 15c., "at what or which place;" from where (in the older use with its sense of "in which position or circumstances") + at.

whereof.x: late 12c., wher-of, "of what? from what source;" mid-13c., "out of which, by means of which;" c. 1300, "of which, of whom;" from where (in the sense of "in which position or circumstances") + of. Similar formation in Swedish hveraf, Danish hvoraf, Dutch waarvan.

whereon.x: c. 1200, wher-on, "on what? about what?"; c. 1300, "upon which, on top of which;" from where (in part in the sense of "in which position or circumstances") + on (adv.).

whereso.x: "in whatever place," late 14c., from where + so. Compare Old English swa hwær swa in same sense. Wheresoever (conj.) "in whatever place in which" is by c. 1200, probably from where + soever.

whereto.x: "to what place or point," c. 1200, wher-to; see where + to.

whicker.x: 1650s, "snigger," imitative (compare snicker). As imitative of a sound made by a horse, from 1753. As the sound of something beating the air, from 1920. Related: Whickered; whickering.

whimper.x: "utter a low, feeble, broken cry," 1510s, probably of imitative origin, or from German wimmern "to whimper, moan." Related: Whimpered; whimpering; whimperingly. The noun is attested by c. 1700; whimpering (n.) is from 1520s.

whipper.x:
1550s, "one who whips," especially in punishment; 1775, "one who wields a driving whip, driver of horses," agent noun from whip (v.).
Whipper-in, "one who drives (hounds) with a whip back into a pack" is attested by 1739. This was extended by 1742 to the member of a political party who summons others to attend on important occasions, hence the modern parliamentary whip (n.).

whippet.x: small, fast type of dog, c. 1600, probably from whip (v.) in the sense of "move quickly" + diminutive suffix -et. Used earlier (1540s) in reference to "a brisk, nimble woman."

whisker.x:
early 15c., "anything that whisks or sweeps" (a fan, fly-swatter, etc.), agent noun from whisk (v.).
As "hair of a man's face" (usually plural), c. 1600, originally a playful extension of this. In reference to animal lip hair, it is recorded from 1670s. Figuratively of a very small difference or space, by 1913. Related: Whiskered; whiskers.

whitish.x: late 14c., "somewhat white, off-white," also a noun; from white (adj.) + -ish. Related: Whitishness.

whitlow.x: "inflammation on a finger or toe," mid-15c., whytlowe, an alteration of whitflaw (late 14c.), from flaw (n.), with first element possibly from Dutch vijt or Low German fit "abscess."

whoopee.x: 1845, "noisy, unrestrained revelry," extended form of whoop, originally American English. The popular song "Makin' Whoopee" is from 1928. The novelty whoopee cushion is from 1931.

widgeon.x: migratory wild duck, 1510s, perhaps from a northern variant of French vigeon, which some trace to Latin vipionem (nominative vipio), "a kind of small crane," a Balearic word, perhaps imitative, with an evolution of form similar to that which produced pigeon. But the French word is later than the English one, and OED (1989) finds all this "very dubious." Also "a fool" (1610s), from proverbial notions of geese. Applied to different species in Europe and in North America.

widower.x: "man who has lost his wife by death and is unremarried," late 14c., widwer, extended from widow (n.). The Old English masc. form was widewa. Similar formation in Middle Dutch weduwer, German Wittwer. Related: Widowerhood.

willies.x: "spell of nervousness," 1896, perhaps from the woollies, a dialectal term for "nervous uneasiness," which is probably in reference to the itchiness of wool garments.

wind-up.x:
1570s, "conclusion or final disposition of some matter," from the verbal phrase (see wind (v.1) + up (adv.)). To wind up (v.) is from c. 1200 as "lift (a bridge, etc.) by a winch;" by mid-15c. as "lift and reset" (a clock's weights). It is by 1590s in the transitive sense of "coil up into a ball or around a bobbin, reel, etc.," likely is the source of the "conclusion" meaning.
To wind up (v.) is attested by c. 1600 as "bring to a state of great tension" (as in wound up), also of a watch or the strings of a musical instrument, hence "set in readiness for action." The baseball arm-movement-before-the-pitch sense is attested by 1906.

windrow.x: "row or line of hay raked together," also of other similar formations, 1520s, from wind (n.1) + row (n.). Because it is exposed to the wind for drying.

wingman.x: pilot of the plane beside the lead aircraft in a formation, 1943 (earlier as a football position), from wing (n.) + man (n.). With figurative extensions, including the dating-sidekick one that was in use by 2006.

wingnut.x: "nut with flared sides for turning with the thumb and forefinger;" so called for its shape (see wing (n.) + nut (n.)). The meaning "weird person" recorded by 1989, probably not from the literal sense but from the secondary sense of nut, influenced perhaps by slang senses of wing in wing-ding "wild party," originally "fit, spasm" (1937). An earlier, British, sense of wingnut was "person with large, protruding ears" (1986). The tendency to use it politically might involve the senses in right-wing, etc.

winless.x: "characterized by an absence of victories," 1948, from win (n.) + -less.

wishful.x: "desirous, longing, having or expressing a wish," 1590s, from wish (n.) + -ful. Related: Wishfully; wishfulness. Earlier in a now obsolete sense of "desirable" (1520s). Wishful thinking is recorded from 1907.

woodcut.x: engraving on wood, or a print made from one, 1660s, from wood (n.) + cut (n.).

workday.x:
"day designated for labor rather than rest or religious observance," also work-day, late 12c., from work (n.) + day (n.). Old English weorcdæg apparently meant "day when work was suspended," as it glosses Latin feria.
As an adjective (c. 1500) it has generally only the literal sense, "of or pertaining to a workday" (compare workaday).

workman.x:
Middle English werkman, from Old English weorcmsnn "hired worker, laborer, one who performs manual tasks;" see work (n.) + man (n.). Similar formation in Dutch werkman, Old Norse verkmaðr.
By c. 1200 as "practitioner of a skilled trade or craft. Workgirl is by 1848 as "girl or young woman engaged in useful manual employment,"

wounder.x: c. 1400, "one who inflicts wounds," agent noun from wound (v.).

wrap-up.x: "summary," 1947, from the verbal phrase; see wrap (v.) + up (adv.). To wrap up "put an end to" is from 1926. To be wrapped up in figuratively (by 1889) is to be bound up with or in or entirely associated with. To be wrapped in error is from c. 1400.

wrapper.x:
late 15c., wrappere, "that with which anything is enclosed" (in oldest reference "piece of fine cloth used for wrapping bread"), agent noun from wrap (v.).
As a type of loose garment for the person, by 1734. In reference to any disposable protective covering by 1808. Specifically as a protective cover for a delivered newspaper, magazine, etc. by 1846.

wrastle.x: an obsolete, dialectal, or vulgar form or pronunciation of wrestle (v.).

wreathe.x:
1520s (transitive), "form by wreathing, form into a wreath," from Middle English wrethen "twist about," from wreath (n.), perhaps also in part from past participle of writhe.
The intransitive sense of "take the form of a wreath, undergo twisting" is by 1580s. Related: Wreathed; wreathing.

wrecker.x:
1804, in reference to one who recovers cargos from wrecked ships, from wreck (n.) + -er (1).
Formerly in Britain often with overtones of "one who causes a shipwreck (by luring a vessel to dangerous coasts) in order to plunder it" (1820). But in 19c. Bahamas and the Florida Keys it could be a legal occupation.
Applied to those who wreck and plunder institutions from 1882. The meaning "demolition worker" is attested by 1958. As a type of ship employed in salvage operations, from 1789. As a railway vehicle with a crane or hoist, from 1904.

wringer.x:
"device for squeezing water from clothes," 1799, agent noun from wring (v.). Earlier of a person whose occupation is to wring clothes after washing (1590s) or wring juice from grapes (late 14c.). Earlier still it meant "miser" or "extortioner" (mid-14c.).
The figurative phrase to put (someone) through the wringer "give a hard time to" is recorded by 1921, American English, earlier as a figurative way to say "dry (someone) out," in reference to the clothes-wringer, which is not properly a "wringer," as the garments are passed between rollers rather than being wrung.

wrongly.x: c. 1300, wrongli, "in a manner contrary to justice, unfairly; wickedly, immorally" (senses now in wrongfully); from wrong (adj.) + -ly (2). By mid-14c as "in an erroneous manner, mistakenly;" 1630s as "inaccurately, incorrectly."

wryneck.x: "common, migratory, woodpecker-like European bird," 1580s, from wry + neck (n.). The bird so called from the singular manner in which it can twist the neck. In pathology as "a twisted, distorted, or stiff neck of a person," by 1753.

wysiwyg.x: by 1972, acronym from what you see is what you get. Picked up by computer programmers and popularized in reference to word-processing, by 1984 the acronym was in advertisements without scare quotes or explanation. Early references note that it is pronounced "wizzy-wig."

waspish.x: "irascible, quick to take offense; spiteful," figurative, 1560s, from wasp + -ish. Shakespeare has wasp-headed. As "resembling or pertaining to a wasp or wasps," by 1590s. Related: Waspishly; waspishness.

wetland.x: "swampy region, area of land suffused with water," 1743, from wet (adj.) + land (n.).

whiffle.x: 1560s, intransitive, "blow in puffs or slight gusts;" 1660s, intransitive, "flicker or flutter as if blown by the wind;" more or less imitative; see waffle (v.) "change course or opinions," and compare whiff. The noun meaning "something light or insignificant" (1670s) is preserved in whiffle-ball (1931).

Wedgwood.x: type of English pottery, by 1787, from Josiah Wedgwood (1730-1795), English potter.

Wellsian.x: by 1912 in reference to the writings of H.G. Wells.

Welshman.x: native of Wales, Middle English Walseman, Walsch man, Wallissheman, from Old English Wilisc mon; see Welsh + man (n.). It was used also by c. 1400 as "male of the indigenous population of later England before the Anglo-Saxon arrival."

Wesleyan.x: "of or pertaining to the Wesley family," 1771, especially in reference to John Wesley (1703-1791), founder of Methodism, and his brother Charles, preacher and prolific hymnist. The surname is from various places in England named West Leigh (or some variant). Related: Wesleyanism.

Winnipeg.x: originally the name of the lake, probably from Ojibwa (Algonquian) winipeg "dirty water;" compare winad "it is dirty." Etymologically related to Winnebago.

walk-out.x: "workers' strike," 1888, U.S. colloquial, from the verbal phrase; see walk (v.) + out (adv.). By 1927 as "act of leaving a meeting in protest." To walk out in a general sense of "to leave" is attested by 1840. To walk out on" a person, "desert, forsake," is by 1913.

war-room.x: "room from which war is directed," also figurative, 1914, from war (n.) + room (n.).

warhorse.x: also war-horse, 1650s, "powerful horse ridden into war," from war (n.) + horse (n.). The figurative sense of "seasoned veteran" of anything is attested by 1828. In reference to women perceived as tough by 1921.

warplane.x: also war-plane, "military combat aircraft," by 1911; see war (n.) + plane (n.2).

wash-out.x:
1873, "excavation by erosion of a roadbed, etc.;" 1877, "act of washing out" (a drain, etc.); from the verbal phrase; see wash (v.) + out (adv.).
The meaning "disappointing failure" is by 1902, perhaps from the verbal phrase wash out "obliterate, cancel, remove" (something written in ink), which is attested from 1570s. Hence also the colloquial sense of "call off (an event) due to bad weather, etc." (1917). To wash in the sense of "blot out, obliterate" is from late 14c.
To wash out "remove (a stain) by washing" is from late 15c.; as "clean the interior of," by 1827. In reference to colored material by 1755, hence washed-out "faded" (1837).

washable.x: 1620s, "that can be used in washing," a sense now obsolete, from wash (v.) + -able. By 1821 as "that can be washed without damage." Related: Washables (n.), 1892.

washdown.x: also wash-down, 1949, "an act of washing; a washing from top to bottom;" from verbal phrase (attested from c. 1600 in reference to food and drink); see wash (v.) + down (adv.).

watchdog.x: also watch-dog, "dog to guard a premise or property," c. 1600; see watch (v.) + dog (n.). The figurative sense is attested by 1845. An older name for a guard-dog was ren-hound (late 12c.), apparently from Old English ærn "house" (see barn).

watchman.x: also watch-man, c. 1400, wacche-man, "guard, sentinel, lookout" (late 12c. as a surname), figuratively "guardian, protector" (mid-15c.), from watch (n.) + man (n.). Also "person characterized by wakefulness" (mid-15c.).

waterway.x: "watercourse, stream," also water-way, mid-15c., water-wei, perhaps from Old English wæterweg, which is of uncertain meaning; see water (n.1) + way (n.). By 1797 specifically as "passage through which vessels enter and depart."

wearable.x: "capable of being worn; fit to be worn," 1580s, from wear (v.) + -able. As a noun, "a garment, piece of wearing apparel" (often wearables) by 1711.

weeklong.x: also week-long, "continuing for a week," 1854, from week + -long.

weepable.x: "deplorable, to be lamented," mid-15c., from weep (v.) + -able. As in weepable victory "a victory joyless or marred by subsequent events."

well-fed.x: "plump, showing results of good feeding," mid-14c., from well (adv.) + past participle of feed (v.).

wheatear.x: type of bird abundant in the Old World, the stone-chat, 1590s, back-formation from white-ears, properly "white-arse" (see white + arse). Said to be so called for its color markings; compare the French name for the bird, cul-blanc, literally "white rump."
also wheat-ear, "an ear of wheat," by early 15c., whete-ere; see wheat + ear (n.2).

whimwham.x: also whim-wham, "whimsical device, trifle, plaything, toy," 1520s, a word of unknown origin; perhaps from Scandinavian (compare Old Norse hvima "to let the eyes wander," Norwegian kvima "to flutter"), or an arbitrary native formation (compare flim-flam, jim-jam, and see higgledy-piggledy).

whitecap.x: 1660s, a common name of birds with light-colored heads, from white (adj.) + cap (n.). Attested from 1773 in reference to breaking waves, from 1818 of mushrooms, and from 1891 in reference to "one of a self-constituted band in U.S. who committed outrages under pretense of regulating public morals" [OED].

whizbang.x: also whiz-bang, whizz-bang, 1915, originally a name among Allied soldiers for a type of German artillery shell in World War I, so called for its characteristic sound. From whizz + bang (n.).

whodunit.x: "murder mystery," 1930, U.S. slang, originally a semi-facetious formation from who done it? Whydunit is from 1968.

whoreson.x: c. 1300, horeson, "bastard son, son of a whore," a term of contempt or abuse, from whore (n.) + son. Often used coarsely but affectionately, it translates Anglo-French fiz a putain. As an adjective, "mean, scurvy, contemptuous," from mid-15c.

wifeless.x: "lacking or bereft of a wife, in a state of bachelorhood," Middle English wifles; see wife (n.) + -less. Old English had wifleas.

wildfowl.x: also wild-fowl, "undomesticated bird," meaning largely birds of the duck tribe, waterfowl collectively, especially a game-bird, late Old English wilde foule; see wild (adj.) + fowl (n.).

wildness.x:
early 14c., "unrestrained behavior, rowdiness" (late 13c. as a surname), from wild (adj.) + -ness. Earlier was wildship (c. 1200).
It is attested by late 14c. as "frenzy;" by mid-15c. as "undomesticated state." The meaning "wilderness, region of unsettled or uncultivated land" is from late 14c. Similar formation in German wildnis.

wind-egg.x: "bad egg, unfertilized or rotten egg," late 14c., from wind (n.1) + egg (n.), on the notion of containing nothing but gas (wind).

windless.x: "out of breath," c. 1400, from wind (n.1) + -less. By 1590s as "unaffected by wind, calm." Related: Windlessly; windlessness.

windpipe.x: "trachea, tube conveying air to and from the lungs," 1520s, from wind (n.1) in the "breath" sense + pipe (n.1).

windsurf.x: also wind-surf, "ride waves on a kind of sailboard," 1969, from wind (n.1) + surf (v.). Related: Windsurfed; windsurfing; windsurfer.

winnable.x: "capable of being won," 1540s, from win (v.) + -able. Related: Winnability.

wiredraw.x: also wire-draw, 1590s, "draw metal out into wires," from wire (n.) + draw (v.). Wiredrawer "maker of wire" is attested by mid-13c. as a surname. Figuratively, "spin out (discourse), lengthen unduly" by 1590s; "stretch, strain, distort, pervert" by c. 1600. Related: Wiredrawing.

wishbone.x: also wish-bone, "furcula of a fowl," 1860, from wish (n.) + bone (n.); so called from the custom of making a wish while pulling the bone in two with another person. The wishbone-breaking custom dates to the early 17c., when the bone was called a merrythought. Also wishing-bone. The U.S. football playing alignment was so called by 1972, from the positions of the backs.

witchery.x: 1540s, "art or practice of witchcraft," from witch (n.) + -ery. By 1580s as "charming or fascinating power."

womanise.x: chiefly British English spelling of womanize (q.v.). Related: Womanised; womanising; womaniser.

womanize.x: 1590s, "make effeminate," from woman + -ize. The sense of "chase women, go wenching" is attested from 1893. Related: Womanized; womanizer; womanizing.

wondrous.x:
"of a nature to excite wonder," c. 1500, formerly also wonderous, probably in part from wonder (n.) + -ous, and partly a substitution for or modification of Middle English wonders (adj.), early 14c., originally the genitive of wonder (n.), with suffix altered by influence of marvelous, etc.
As an adverb, "wonderfully," from 1550s. Compare wonderful. Related: Wondrously; wondrousness.

woodcock.x: common long-beaked European bird esteemed as food and a test of the sportsman's skill, Middle English wodecok, from Old English wuducocc, from wudu (see wood (n.)) + coc (see cock (n.1)). Applied later to a smaller North American bird of similar general characteristics.

woodpile.x: also wood-pile, "stack of wood," 1550s, from wood (n.) + pile (n.1).

woodshed.x: "shed for keeping wood as fuel," 1799, from wood (n.) + shed (n.1). Sometimes a euphemism for "outhouse." Figuratively, as the place for private punishment of a child, by 1883, American English colloquial.

woodside.x: also wood-side, "edge of a forest," c. 1300, from wood (n.) + side (n.).

woodsman.x:
1680s, "one who dwells in or frequents the woods," from woods (see wood (n.)) + man (n.).
Earlier was woodman (early 15c.), "one adept at hunting in woods," also an official forester, appointed to tend the royal woods. Also "wild or savage person" (late 14c., Old English had wudu-mann), but this is perhaps from or influenced by wood (adj.).

woodward.x: late Old English, "forester, land-reeve," hence the surname; etymologically "keeper of a wood;" see wood (n.) + ward (n.).

woodwind.x: 1876, from wood (n.) + wind (n.1) in the musical instrument sense. Related: Woodwinds.

woodwork.x:
mid-15c., "carpentry;" 1640s, "article or part of an object made of wood;" from wood (n.) + work (n.).
"That which is produced by carpenters' or joiners' art," especially wooden details of a house, hence figurative phrase come (or crawl) out of the woodwork, by 1960, suggestive of cockroaches, etc.

wordbook.x: also word-book, "book containing words and their explanations in alphabetical order," 1590s, perhaps modeled on German Wörterbuch; see word (n.) + book (n.).

wordless.x: c. 1200, wordles, "ineffable; indescribable or inexpressible in words," from word (n.) + -less. By c. 1500 as "silent, speechless." Related: Wordlessly; wordlessness.

wordplay.x: also word-play, "play on words," 1855; see word (n.) + play (v.).

workable.x: "that can be worked or is worth working," 1540s, from work (v.) + -able. Related: Workably; workableness; workability.

workaday.x: c. 1200, werkedei (n.), "a working day, day designated for labor rather than religious observance or rest," from Old Norse virkr dagr "working day;" see work (n.) + day (n.). Obsolete as a noun, it passed into an adjective mid-16c., "relating to working days," hence "plodding, toiling."

workroom.x: also work-room, "room for working," by 1828, from work (n.) + room (n.).

wormhole.x: also worm-hole, 1590s, "hole made by a burrowing insect" (in fruit, timber, etc.), from worm (n.) + hole (n.). Astrophysics sense is attested from 1957. Related: Wormholed.

wormwood.x:
perennial herb of Europe and northern Asia, used in medicinal preparations and having a proverbially bitter aftertaste; by late 14c., worm wode, a folk etymologizing of Old English wermod "wormwood, absinthe," which is related to vermouth, but the ultimate etymology is unknown. Compare Old Saxon wermoda, Dutch wermoet, Old High German werimuota, German Wermut.
Weekley suggests wer "man" + mod "courage," from its early use as an aphrodisiac. Century Dictionary suggests werian + mod, as though "protect-mind." Figurative use, however, is usually in reference to what is bitter and undesirable.
Perhaps because of the folk etymology, it formerly was regarded as a vermifuge and used to protect clothes and bedding from moths and fleas.
 A medecyne for an hawke that hath mites. Take the Iuce of wormewode and put it ther thay be and thei shall dye. ["Book of St. Albans," 1486]

wrangler.x: 1510s, "one who takes part in quarrels, angry debater, stubborn adversary," agent noun from wrangle (v.). The meaning "person in charge of horses or cattle, herder on a Western ranch" is from 1888; as a proprietary name for a brand of jeans, trademarked 1947, claiming use from 1929.

wreckage.x: 1814, "fact or process of being wrecked, act of wrecking," from wreck (v.) + -age. The meaning "remains of a wrecked thing" is from 1832.

write-in.x: "unlisted candidate whose name is inserted in a ballot by a voter," by 1932, American English, from the verbal phrase (late 14c. as "insert in writing;" by 1932 in the ballot sense); see write (v.) + in (adv.).

write-up.x: "written account or description," by 1882, from the verbal phrase; see write (v.) + up (adv.). To write up is attested by early 15c. as "put (a full account) in writing." It is by c. 1500 as "enter (someone's) name in a list or roll" for a particular purpose.

Waterford.x: city in southeastern Ireland; by 1783 in reference to a type of glassware manufactured there.

Wilsonian.x: by 1921, "characteristic of the U.S. presidency of Woodrow Wilson" (1856-1924), especially in reference to idealism in foreign policy.

Winnebago.x: Siouan people of eastern Wisconsin, 1766, from Potawatomi winepyekoha, literally "person of dirty water," in reference to the muddy or fish-clogged waters of the Fox River below Lake Winnebago. As a type of motor vehicle, attested from 1966.

Wurlitzer.x: type of musical instrument (originally a player piano popular in silent movie theaters, later a type of jukebox), 1925, named for The Wurlitzer Company, founded near Cincinnati, Ohio, in 1856 by Rudolph Wurlitzer (1831-1914), Saxon immigrant to U.S. An importer at first, he started production of pianos in 1880; coin-operated pianos in 1896.

wetback.x: "illegal Mexican immigrant to the U.S.," c. 1924, from wet (adj.) + back (n.); from notion of wading the Rio Grande.

waistcoat.x: also waist-coat, 1510s, used of various garments, originally one without sleeves worn by men under the cloak; from waist + coat (n.).

walk-over.x:
in sports, "easy victory," 1838, such as one that happens in the absence of competitors, when the solitary starter, being obliged to complete the event, can traverse the course at a walk. Usually of horse racing.
The transferred sense of "anything accomplished with great ease" is attested from 1902.
To walk (all) over (someone) "treat with contempt" is from 1851, a separate development.

wallboard.x: "flat piece of manufactured building material used for surfacing walls and ceilings," 1912, American English, from wall (n.) + board (n.1).

washboard.x:
also wash-board, hardwood board with a corrugated or other surface on which clothes are rubbed for cleansing, 1882 (washing-board is by 1810), from wash (v.) + board (n.1).
As a percussion instrument, attested by 1925; as an image of a rough road by 1934. In reference to abdominal muscles, by 1950 in boxing jargon. Earlier such muscle development was described as checkerboard (1893).

washed-up.x: "no longer effective," 1923, theater slang, from notion of washing up at the end of a performance job; see wash (v.) + up (adv.). Said to have been picked up next in boxing slang. Hence wash up "bring to a conclusion" (1925). As a noun, wash-up is by 1884 as "act of washing table utensils;" 1887 as "act of washing oneself."

wasteland.x:
1825 as one word, from waste (adj.) + land (n.). Compare French terrain vague "waste ground" (used in English by 1920). Figurative sense is attested from 1868. Eliot's poem is from 1922.
 April is the cruellest month, breeding 
 Lilacs out of the dead land, mixing 
 Memory and desire, stirring 
 Dull roots with spring rain.

watchable.x: 1610s, "subject to watching," from watch (v.) + -able. By 1933 of movies, etc., "that may be watched with pleasure." Related: Watchability.

watchword.x: also watch-word, c. 1400, wacce-word, "military password, word or phrase used to identify oneself to a sentry or guard," from watch (n.) in the military sense of "period of standing guard duty" + word (n.). In the non-military sense of "motto, slogan" it dates from 1738.
